speechtext:
The House resumed from Thursday, May 20, the debate on ,the motion of Sir Henry Drayton (Minister of Finance), that Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of Ways and Means and the proposed amendment thereto of Hon. W. S. Fielding.
Mr. A. B. MeCOIG (Kent, Ont.): Mr. Speaker, representing in this House, as I have the privilege of doing, one of the largest urban and rural ridings, if not the largest, in the Dominion of Canada, I wish to give to the House a few reasons why 1 purpose supporting the amendment of my hon. friend the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) to the Budget which was presented to the House a few days ago by the hon. the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton). I wish as well to offer a few objections to some of the arguments which were advanced by hon. gentlemen who addressed the House from the Government side and to give a few reasons why I take exception to the views which they presented. Mr. Speaker, with your long parliamentary experience and knowledge of the different members

of this House personally you *would have been amused as you sat in your place and listened to the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) who spoke with a brief for the great Mas-sey-Harris corporation, advocating their case and telling us why we should not allow agricultural implements to come into Canada in opposition to theirs.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I have very great doubt as to whether the hon. gentleman is in order in imputing to another hon. gentleman the circumstance that he holds a brief for a manufacturing corporation. I have very grave doubt indeed as to whether the hon. gentleman would be in order in making an assertion of that kind unless he were to do so in a constitutional manner.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
That expression, as I understand, is only used as a figure of speech.
Mr. MeCOIG: If it would be more in order that the word "brief" should be withdrawn I will withdraw it and say that he was advocating their case. With all due respect to that hon. gentleman, when he undertakes to interfere with any policy that may be advocated by any hon. gentleman in this House, which has for its object the admission of agricultural implements into this country in order to give us greater food supply, those who have the real cause of the plain people of this land at heart should object to the statement the hon. gentleman made, and should do their utmost to put an end to the great contribution that some manufacturers are securing from the people of Canada at the present time. In justification of this statement let me draw the attention of the House to a despatch in the Globe from the city of Washington which states that this year the wheat crop in the United States will be 483,000,000 bushels as against a crop of 731,000,000 bushels last year. This shows that we are going to be confronted with a great shortage of wheat on the part of the United States. We have an Associated Press despatch fro-m old England which states that the British people will receive fro-m the North American continent 4,000,000 tons less wheat than they received last year. I also want to draw the attention of Parliament and the country to the fact that we are face to face with scarcity, it may not be too much to say that we are possibly on the threshold of a wheat famine. This Parliament should do everything possible to assist the producers of this land in getting every bushel of grain so that they may reap as large a 167
harvest as possible to assist the other nations of the world with what we do not need for home consumption.
Let me go further, Sir. We have the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) standing up and advocating protection to-day because he represents- in this House one of the large cities in the province of Ontario. But it was only a few years ago, in 191-1, that the same hon. gentleman was running in a rural riding on the reciprocity platform and advocating the very thing which he seems to be opposing to-day. May we not therefore say: "Oh, consistency thou art a jewel"? At a late hour last night we heard the hon. member -for Fraser Valley (Mr. Stacey). How he tickled the ears of the high protectionists, and the representatives of the corporations, or rather the stockholders of the corporations-I should rather put it in that form. How they applauded and pounded their desks when the hon. member complimented the Government because they had placed a duty of ninety cents a barrel on apples-a food, Sir, which the people require so badly and which in the old days so many families in humble circumstances could enjoy. The effect of this duty on apples was brought home to me in a convincing form last night when in company with -another gentleman I took a walk down Sparks street. Then I understood the reason for the applause with which the remarks of the hon. member for Fraser Valley were greeted. My friend and I dropped into a fruit store and what did we see there? A sign that apples were selling at the rate of three for 25 cents. Fancy, Sir, three apples for a quarter, and hon. gentlemen opposite were pounding their desks because of the fact that the apple growers were getting a protection of ninety cents a barrel! Fancy people in humble circumstances being forced to pay such a price for fruit which they so greatly need, instead of being able to obtain it at a reasonable figure. I am interested in fruit-growing to a limited extent. I set out some fruit trees in my orchard last year, and propose to do the same again this year; but I say, Sir, that if the customs duty compels the plain people of Canada to pay so much for fruit let that duty be removed in order that fruit-which after all is a food-may be available to them at the very lowest possible cost.
We had also yesterday a lengthy address from the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). We listened to him for an hour before dinner and then for another hour when the House resumed after recess. The hon. member attacked the United Farm-



ers, and what did he say? He said to them: " You people have stores in the West. You supply agricultural implements to purchasers out there and demand the cash." Then the hon. member grew eloquent and he addressed compliments to the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt), whose face lighted up at the compliments that were paid to him. The hon. member for Brantford was held up as a public benefactor who supplied the farmer of the West with his wares and granted him six months, two years, and sometimes three years, to pay for them. Is it not a grand thing that we should have in this House a manufacturer who is so generous that he is willing to sell the machinery which he produces on lengthy payments? But did the hon. member for Vancouver Centre state that the hon. member for Brantford's firm-the International Harvester Company-and also the Massey-Harris Company, when they sell machinery to the farmers in the West or in other parts of the country, expect those farmers to pay at the rate of from eight to twelve per cent per annum for every day they give them on the goods which they supply. Furthermore, Sir, on some occasions, on some of the implements these firms supply, when the customer wants time, they advance the price from $50 to $75, and add interest to the price besides. Is it not significant that these gentlemen are united together and are all agreed upon the one great question of extracting from the people of this country every possible dollar they can, and likewise charging them for the time allowed in paying for the goods?
The hon. member for Vancouver Centre brought forward one question which is of vital importance to the people, and on which I agree with him to a very large extent, and that is the question of the Wheat Board. That hoard, I wish to assure the Government, does not meet with the approval of the farmers in that section of Ontario which I have the privilege of representing, and for reasons which I will furnish later. In the meantime let me say that the hon. member for Vancouver Centre certainly did pay his compliments to the United Farmers in this regard. He almost charged them with responsibility for the creation of the Wheat Board, but he omitted to state that it was the Government, and not the United Farmers that created the W'heat Board. Some time ago, in reply to a question, the Minister of Trade and Commerce stated that the participation certificates would likely yield the wheat growers about forty cents a 
bushel. The Wheat Board in the first place exacted on every bushel of wheat that is sold in this country fifteen cents, in the second place twenty-five cents, and in the third instance forty cents, making a total of eighty cents. Thus, if the eighty cents a bushel is received on the wheat, and the participation certificates only amount to forty cents in the way of return to the producer, it is going to cost the Canadian farmer forty cents for every bushel of wheat that has been handled and sold by the Wheat Board in Canada. If this is true, then figuring on the basis of five bushels of wheat to every barrel of flour, if the consumers of Canada had got their wheat at what the farmers sold it for they would have been able to purchase their flour at $2 a barrel less than they have had to pay for it. This, Sir, I believe, is one of the reasons the people of Canada are opposed to the Wheat Board, and why they are to a very large extent agreed that it should be wiped out of existence at the earliest possible moment.
Let me go a step further in this matter. As far as regards the province of Ontario, the Wheat Board have been taking the wheat from that province and not allowing the millers to grind it, which has resulted in driving many of the stock raisers of Ontario out of the stock-raising business. Those stock raisers would have been able to obtain the offal from the wheat had the millers of Ontario only been allowed to operate and been permitted to sell the flour they could have made instead of shipping away the wheat to be ground in other countries. What does that mean? It means, Sir, that in the province of Ontario for months at a time, the wheels of the flour mills including many of the largest, have not been turning; in the different localities many men have been deprived of employment; and the stock raisers have been driven out of business to an extent that will be illustrated by some figures which I shall now quote.
These figures are taken from the stockyards report as set forth in the Toronto Globe, and they relate to stock that was placed in the Toronto stockyards for the first three months of the present year, and the corresponding months of last year. Of cattle there were 72,766 head in 1920. In the corresponding three months of last year there were 90,183 head, making a difference of nearly 18,000 less cattle sold in those stockyards this year than was the case in 1919. Of swine there w'ere 95,285 for the first three months of the present

year, and 139,969 for the corresponding period of last year, a difference of nearly 45,000 hogs. I ask you, what will that mean to the consumers of this country? Of sheep there were 14,083 this year, and 26,764 last year, a difference of 12,000 less sheep in the first three- months of the present year. What does that mean, Sir? It means that on account of the wheat being shipped from this country instead of being ground here, stock raisers have been deprived of the offal to enable them to finish their stock and place it on the markets of Canada.
Now let me give figures to further show the extent to which these men are going out of the stock-raising business. Taking calves, there were 2,500 more calves sold in Toronto for the first three months this year than were sold for the corresponding period last year; whereas if the farmers of Ontario had the offal and had the feed which they should have been able to obtain they would have been able to finish a large proportion af these calves, and in placing them on the market been able to contribute materially to the available food supply of the country. I therefore feel on safe ground in advising the Government to hesitate before they permit	the Wheat
Board to remain any longer in charge of the supplies which are being produced by	the farmers	of Canada.
Objection to the Wheat Board has been directed, so far as supporters of the Government are concerned, not only by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), who has looked thoroughly into the question. We see that the representative of the Government to England and also to Washington, in the person of Mr. Lloyd Harris, is also attacking the board. At a dinner given in Hamilton the other day that gentleman is reported as follows:
Mr. Harris alluded to the Board of Commerce being appointed to check profiteering, and stated that whi-le it was at this duty, the Wheat Board was profiteering to " beat the band." If he were allowed to control the entire steel output of Canada he could make all kinds of money, and the situation regarding wheat was like this. The board made wheat prices that were a crime.
Now, Sir, if the trade representative of the Government to England says that the Wheat Board is profiteering to beat the band and that the prices they made for wheat are a crime, then am I not justified in appealing to the Government to give the matter a great deal more serious consideration than they have evidenced up to the present time? The statement is also made that the Board of Commerce is at present 167$
investigating the operations of the profiteers of the country. In this connection I would recall to the House the day the Board of Commerce was created. You will remember, Sir, that hon. members on this side of the House protested against the creation of the Board of Commerce, advancing the argument that we had too many commissions at the expense of the people of Canada. We protested against the Board of Commerce on the ground that we ought to have a public prosecutor in the country whose duty it would be to investigate all cases of profiteering andi to bring before the county judges all persons against whom charges could be made. We contended that profiteers could be prosecuted in that manner with less expense to the people of Canada. That was our stand then, so far as I am concerned, I can say that it is my attitude yet in regard to this subject. The Department of Finance now have offenders in connection with the Income Tax or	the Business Profits Tax
brought	before the	county courts
through the medium of their officers, thus obviating a great deal of unnecessary expenditure, and there is no reason why a similar procedure should not be followed in the case of profiteers. The Board of Commerce, Mr. Speaker, has issued a new circular which it would take too long a time for me to read. This circular is issued to every grocer of the country, and in warm weather like this I am afraid it will prove too laborious a task for the already hard-worked man behind the counter to read what is contained in it. There is a long list of requirements as to what these people shall and shall not do, what they pay for their goods, what they sell them for, what profits they receive, and all information as to whether they are profiteering or not. It is quite a voluminous document. Could you imagine a more ridculous letter sent out to the trade, Sir? Here is a list of articles, eighty in number, which has to be made out every month. Why, Sir, are the Government going to let this board run wild? Are they going to allow the board to inconvenience beyond all reason people who are transacting business honestly, requiring them to have special clerks to keep track of every article taken in and sold and every cent of profit which is made? If eo, the expense of additional clerks which will have to be borne by the consumer will greatly enhance the price of goods. Thl* body has been in existence for nearly a year investigating profiteering, but it has not yet succeeded in putting one profiteer in jail;

These are, to a very large extent, the reasons why I am on this occasion assuring the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) that I will support his amendment and any other amendment brought in by any hon. member for the purpose of assisting in reducing the tariff on the necessaries of life, so as to give us every opportunity of producing as much as possible with a view to making the cost of living in this country as cheap as possible to the Canadian consumers.
Mr. JOHN A. MAHARG (Maple Creek): Mr. Speaker, before entering into a discussion of the Budget, I should like to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) on his frankness in laying before Parliament and the people of Canada the exact situation in which we find ourselves from a financial point of view. I should also like to congratulate him on what appears to me to be a brave attempt in some respects to secure additional revenue. I cannot go so far as to congratulate him on all of the methods he proposes in order to secure this revenue; I only wish I could. No doubt, he is making an honest attempt to curtail extravagant expenditure; but as the hon. member for Kent (Mr. McCoig) has said, the relief he hopes to give to some and his belief that those more able to pay will be called upon to do so, will, I am afraid fall far short of the mark. His estimates of values of goods when they become luxuries or not real necessities, might apply to warmer climates; but they are, in the main, rather too low for a country with the temperatures we have. They may, however, be, in his opinion, the right values to put on these goods, and we shall leave the matter at that. He might have gone just a little further, and while he purposes making those pay who are able to do so, he might have made it a little easier for those to whom he wishes to afford relief to get along. His Budget makes no provision for lowering the daily or monthly cost of living of the average workingman, the average individual, be he a labourer

in town or a labourer on the farms. This Budget will not make any reduction in the monthly bills of such a man; on the contrary, I believe it will increase them to a certain extent, and I do not think that is what the minister purposed doing. He might have gone a little further and substantially reduced, if not entirely wiped out the tariff on the necessaries of life, particularly as regards foodstuffs. We, as producers of food, which is practically our entire production, are quite prepared to give the consumer the entire world for his market in which to buy his necessaries of life so far as food is concerned. The Minister of Finance might also have gone a little further and made some reductions in the tariff on other necessaries of life. Taking into consideration the climatic conditions he might have made it easier for a man to keep his family warm during the long winter months we 'have in this country. I will not dwell on this matter any further than to draw attention to the fact that the Budget of the Minister of Finance is not going to accomplish what I think he intends it should do.
Another point that I wish to touch on, apart from the Budget entirely, is this, namely, that the discussion that has taken place and the sources that it has come from in this House must surely furnish food for thought for the average individual in 'Canada. We have heard the statement made that political expediency has largely governed the actions of Government as well as of individuals in this country; and when we see men who in former years were ardent supporters of tariff reductions taking, as the hon. member for Kent (Mr. McCoig) has just stated, a complete somersault and now advocating protection, there must be something worthy of consideration at the bottom of the matter. We have often heard it stated that a certain number of Liberals remain within the Liberal party in order that they may control that party. I am not going to say whether that is true or not. The year 1911 brough a number of that type of Liberals to the front and their position became clear, and I hope 1920 will bring the balance, if there are any, to the front, so that the people of Canada may know exactly where-they stand. Such disclosures are being made from time to time, and the position of a number of such Liberals has been disclosed. There may be obvious reasons for this. We hear of large mergers taking place these days and of certain concerns represented by certain hon. gentlemen being interested in those mergers, and there may be something in that.
We shall, however, leave the matter at that, and no doubt time will disclose just to what extent that condition of affairs exists.
1 desire to touch briefly on the remarks of one or two hon. members who have taken part in this debate. In the first place, I want to deal briefly with a few oif the remarks made by the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Man-ion) who, I am glad, is in his seat, although I can assure him I am not going to say anything that will be annoying to him. While addressing the House my hon. friend gave us a large number of comparisons of conditions, his remarks and his comparisons being almost entirely as regards the Mother Country, Germany and the United States. He held Germany and the United States up as models, England on the other hand being in every case at the bottom. He gave us figures and percentages without end, but his figures and percentages amount to absolutely nothing unless the full conditions are understood. He first dealt with the wheat production and importation of Great Britain in an endeavour to show that Great Britain did not compare with other European countries, of which he mentioned several, in the matter of production of wheat. He stated, if I understood him aright, that during the year previous to the war Great Britain imported 215,009,000 bushels of wheat and produced 57,000,000 bushels, making a total of 272,000,000 bushels. The House will readily see that Great Britain did not import all that wheat for her own consumption; otherwise, she would have been consuming per capita almost double as much wheat as any other country in the world. Canada is considered one of the largest consumers of wheat, and our consumption is in the neighbourhood of five bushels per capita. What did Great Britain do with that wheat? I want to tell the hon. gentleman that he has no doubt eaten some of that wheat [DOT] that was imported into the Old Country, ground into flour, made into biscuits, and sold to him in his own city at a price equal to, if not less than, the .Canadian-made article. That is one of Great Britain's ways of doing business. She thrives on this importation and exportation, and it is that which has made het what she is. I just give that illustration to show that unless you have all the figures and understand fully the conditions, such a huge array of percentages and figures as the hon. member gave count for nothing.
I might go a little further. The hon. gentleman-and I am very sorry he made thi3 comparison-endeavoured to hold Great

Britain up as a land almost of paupers. He mentioned the thousands and thousands of paupers there -were in that country, and in his comparison he took the year 1914 for England and the year 1910 for the United States. Now we all recollect very well what hardships there were in our own country in 1914, and how in 1910 this country was flourishing as it had not done before for years. But in 1912 and 1913, which is about the period the hon. ' gentleman took for England, we find that in our own country municipalities and provinces were furnishing funds to give employment. I know of hundreds of thousands of tons of rock being crushed, even though it could not be used at the time, but was merely piled up, in order to give employment to our people. I think the hon. gentleman should have taken these conditions into consideration in making his comparison.

There are paupers and paupers, and some countries do not worry very much about them until the paupers are amongst them, in the curb or some other similar place, when institutions have to !be provided for them. Other countries let people shift for themselves and keep no records of their paupers. This should be borne in mind when studying the hon. gentleman's comparison.
The hon. gentleman also compared the railways of England with those of other countries, [DOT] and here again, unless the actual conditions are understood, figures and percentages count for nothing. He instanced the capitalization per mile of railroads in England. Probably the hon. gentleman has travelled more miles in England than I have, and he must have observed that there is absolutely no>
comparison between the roadbed 'and facilities along the railroads in England, which he tried to show up in their worst light, and those in the United States or Canada. The roadbed of the railroads in England and the speed at which the trains go is absolutely different from the conditions that prevail in this country. Were the light trains that are used on the roads in England hurled across our roads
[Mr. Maharg.l
at the speed at which they go there, they would be in the ditch before they had got up speed. He must also remember that it is service that counts. To give only one illustration, the roads running into the city of London bring in almost as many people to work each day as there are in the city itself. Millions of people are brought in to the city in the morning to work, and are taken out in the evening. The roads there are built for service and they give service, and where you get service, rates are a secondary consideration. The hon. gentleman also gave the cost per ton mile. Here again his comparison was entirely misleading, unless you are familiar with the conditions. Let me give just one illustration: Previous to the war it cost more to take a bushel or a carload of wheat across the province of Saskatchewan toy short haul, similar to what they have in England, than it took to transport it from the province of Saskatchewan to the port of Liverpool. That shows that it is the length of haul that counts, and not the circumstances as the hon. gentleman gave them.

His comparisons related to the period previous to the war for the most part, and he made no comparisons with what England did after the war started, when the great morale which the hon. gentleman has spoken of in these protected countries was put to a very severe test. What do we find Great Britain did after the war started? The very first thing she did was to send over to the continent her "Contemptible Little Army"-as described by a German officer-of 300,000 men, which held back the Germans for days and

weeks and months. It was only
4 p.m. a short time afterwards, that free-trade Britain was financing these high-tariff countries which the hon. gentleman referred to the other day. Great Britain kept on financing them out of her own resources, and loaned money to them to a far greater amount than her borrowings from the United States. Great Britain did more than that. She broke the back of Germany while that other country which the hon. gentleman used in his comparison stood looking on, almost to the finish. It reminds me of a little incident I happened to witness once in a home. A mouse had made its appearance in the kitchen, where a little girl of tender years and her father happened to be at the time. While the father undertook to catch the mouse the little girl safely perched herself on a chair, and after he had succeeded in catching and killing the mouse, the little girl at once called to her mother upstairs "we have got the mouse." That was very much the position that country which he was comparing to England was in at the close of the war. What is England doing to-day? We could give comparison after comparison with the little free trade country that was held up and which came out of the bottom of the list but which holds a. very prominent position no matter in what respect you may wish to compare it. The hon. gentleman made comparisons as to the advancement of agriculture in Great Britain. What has Great Britain had to do since she adopted the free trade policy? She has had to break down and she has broken down to a certain extent, the greatest land monopoly that any country ever had to contend with. First of all she had to ' break down the system and get possession of the land. What did she do in connection with Ireland? She spends hundreds of millions of pounds for the purchase of land on behalf of the agriculturists of Ireland. England had to break down this isystem before she could start building up again. Great Britain is not recognized as a producer of cereals. She is a land of pasturage; it does not pay her to produce cereals and she only turned to the production of cereals owing to the necessities of [DOT]war, and no country, not even Canada or
the United States, has increased its production of food stuffs to a greater extent than did Great Britain during the years of the war. I do not think we need go any farther. It was not because she could not do it but because there were better lines of business for her to follow.
I do not wish to take up too much of the time of the House but there were one or *two remarks of some other hon. gentlemen that I wish to refer to. The hon. gentleman who has just preceded me (Mr. Mc-Coig) has relieved me of considerable trouble in this respect, but he did not go quite far enough in some lines. The hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) yesterday gave us very largely a repetition-of what we got at our last regular session in regard to the farmers' movement. That was answered pretty fully, I think, at that [DOT]time, and I am not going to detain the House with a repetition of what was said then. Once is surely enough. But he made further some statements that are not correct and which I intend to deal with. The hon. gentleman who has preceded me touched on one of these and that is the Wheat Board. We did not ask for the Wheat Board. The inference, if not the statement is to the effect that the farmers asked for the Wheat Board. One hon. member described it as the pooling of our wheat. While the hon. member from Kent (Mr. MeCoig) stated that the Government appointed the Wheat Board I want to go further and say that the Government did it against the strong opposition of the farmers [DOT]of this country. The farmers did not want it and they did not ask for it. But if the Government stepped in, took possession and broke down the lines which had been built up financially and otherwise, and if there is pooling in the buying of wheat overseas, we have no hesitation in saying that we consider it the proper course for our Government to carry out pooling in the selling of wheat, just so long at least as there was pooling in buying from us. We know where this comes from, we know whom the hon. gentleman from Vancouver Centre is speaking for. He is speaking for those who want to get back to the old speculative methods of dealing in wheat. We know who they are and to what lengths the ramifications of their influence extend. They have secured possession of a portion of the press of Western Canada, they have got their tentacles into almost every branch of western business. Behind this movement is a most powerful company, and what has been said by this hon. gentleman

is only an echo of the editorials appearing in the press controlled by them, and it is about time the people of this country knew why this campaign was being carried on and why the hon. gentleman is knocking the farmers' movement. It is simply to make it possible for the speculators to get back into action and to mulct the consumers as well as the producers in connection with the marketing of grain. The present system is in the interest not only of the producer but of the consumer. Just so long as the pooling arrangement exists on the other side where our wheat is marketed, we must have a similar arrangement here; if governments are going to [DOT]buy the governments will have to sell.
There was one other remark that was made yesterday to which I wish t-o refer. An hon. gentleman undertook to castigate the farmers rather severely and to say that they were dealing in American implements only. He is right to a certain extent. There is no doubt that they are dealing in American implements very largely, but there is a reason for it. Twelve or fourteen years ago we organized a 'company-not the company that was spoken of here yesterday but a local company- to handle necessaries in connection with our farms such as implements and so on, but not necessarily retail shelf goods. We organized and incorporated that company, but what did we find? We found that there was not a Canadian manufacturer who would sell us one agricultural implement of any kind. You could not even buy a hand cultivator. We had to go to the United States. We had to go as far south as Tennessee to buy a plough. And what did we find? We found that we could buy a three-furrow (plough, pay freight and duty into our country and sell that plough at less than we had been paying for a two-furrow plough. That is the exact situation. If any gentleman wants to blame us for that, well and good; we are quite prepared to justify our action in doing what we did. We were the victims of circumstances, we had to do it and we did it. The manufacturers say that we must have a tariff to raise revenue. If that is a fact, how are you going to get your revenue if you do not go outside and buy a few of the articles that you require? It is absolutely inconsistent, because if you have to get a revenue in that way you have to import. However, that was not the reason in this case; we went out of the country simply because the manufacturers in this country absolutely refused to sell to us.

I cannot agree with the Budget now before the House in many respects. In some respects I believe it is along the right line but it does not go far enough to meet the conditions of the country at the present time. I hope the minister may see fit during the consideration of the resolutions in committee to make some changes. I have 6poken to him about some changes that he agrees with me would be only fair and when the resolutions come into committee we will look into these matters. I am not going to touch upon them at this particular time as I have the assurance of the minister that if there is any unfairness it will be dealt with, and I am quite prepared to take the minister at his word.
As to the feeling in the country towards the Budget I have been travelling a little recently; I have been in some of the Ontario centres within the last day or two; and have been talking to a lot of people. They were not farmers, they were business and professional men, following different professions, some were labour men. I asked them for no information whatever; it was all volunteered to me. Both the professional man and the labouring man informed me that this Budget afforded no relief to them, not even to the labouring. man, but that it was going to make it harder for them. I hope the minister will take into consideration the values that he has placed on some of these articles when we are in committee. I think that the minister's valuation is too low on some things. I do not care how hard he hits some articles that are really luxuries, and that are not indispensable to the community; but with respect to wearing apparel, boots and shoes, and similar articles, I am convinced that it is not economical buying at the present time to purchase below the figures which the minister has named.

Mr. Speaker, there appears to be no response from hon. gentleman opposite; therefore we on this side will continue the debate, as the last word on this question has not yet been uttered. I listened with much interest on Tuesday last to the speech of the Minister of Finance dealing with the condition of the country and the financial proposals of the Government. In commencing my remarks I wish to congratulate the minister on his decision to stop borrowing and in future to pay bis way. The financial methods in vogue in this country during the last four

or five years, by which the public debt has been rolling up like a snowball, were a matter of grave concern to every man who cared about the future of the country. The task of my hon. friend at this period of our history is not an easy one. In addition to providing for the war debt, it falls to his lot to teach the rudiments of economy to an Administration that has always been accustomed to "dash away and spend the money." This habit of extravagance they contracted before my hon. friend became a member of the ministry. We on this side sympathize with the minister in the position in which he is placed, and would like to help him if wti could. It must be a very uncomfortable experience to be seated on an empty chest by the side of bottomless deficits fishing for a Budget. The Government professes to stand for economy in theory, why not also stand for economy in practice? In the remarks that I am about to make regarding the expenditures of the Government it may appear as though 1 were attacking the Administration. This is not my purpose. My main object is to give my humble contribution in the direction of checking the prevailing extravagance and preventing waste. The real friends of the Government are the men who tell them the truth; the worst enemies they have are the people who flatter them. I see no good reason why this Government should be immune from criticisms. It is far from pei-fect. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell)-who comes nearer to being a saint than any of the rest of the ministers - does not claim perfection.

speechtext:
unknown quantity. The electorate requires a guide, a policy, an association with those who invite its confidence; and the Government offers neither guidance nor principles, nor familiarity with the people. The situation is not suddenly precipitated. It began with the conclusion of the war, since when futile efforts at permanent coalition have more than once been made, and minister after minister has dropped out with no successor to his place, until the situation has become difficult for the Government and despondent to its supporters.
Now, Sir, we have here a picture of a chicken with its head off, gasping and winking its eye to make believe it is still alive. That is an extraordinary picture to come from a friendly newspaper which had a great deal to do with bringing this Union Government into existence. The Gazette tells us that this is a leaderless ministry destitute of policy and the despair of its friends. That is strong language, hut no one in Canada is in a better position to know the facts than the Montreal Gazette. Other newspapers have been even more emphatic than the Gazette, but the Government pay no attention. I have in my desk a very interesting little book which I found in the library. The title is, "Recreations of an Historian." It was written by George M. Trevallyan. He describes an after dinner discussion in London many years ago participated in by a number of eminent literary men, of whom Thomas Carlyle was one. The question was whether protests in the press and in books have any effect on public conduct. These philosophers decided among themselves that these public protests and criticisms had no effect whatever. They simply read them and then threw them into some thirty-two-dollar waste-paper basket and forget all about them. Carlyle who' had been silent up to that moment, took his pipe out of his mouth and made the following remark:
There was a man once named Rousseau who wrote a hook on political questions. The nobles of that country laughed, but the next edition was bound in their skins.
It occurred to me that something like that, in a figurative sense might happen to the present Government. Now, Sir, the people have been asked to produce and save and many of them are honestly trying to do so. But what About the Government? War expenditure is inevitable, but what excuse can there be for increasing the ordinary expenditures of the Government by over $100,000,000 during the past year? Can there be any excuse for that enormous addition to our public expenditure? Now here are the figures. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance at page 2661 of Hansard the other day told us that the expenditure on ordin-

ary account for the year ending March 31, 1920, was 1336,741,110. Not one dollar of this is for war. When we turn to Public Accounts, page 9, for last year's expenditures, that is, for the year ending 31st March, 1919, we find the expenditure on ordinary account to be $232,731,282. Subtract the one from the other and you have an addition to our expenditure for the past year over the former year of $104,009,828. When the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) last year told us that any further cash advance to the soldiers would bankrupt the country, every one expected that the knife would be applied. But, Mr. Speaker, economy seems to be a despised and forgotten thing so far as this Administration is concerned. I have read to you a quotation from the Gazette. Now I want to call another friendly witness. The hon. member for Colchester (Mr. McCurdy) in his New Year's message to the people of Nova Scotia used the following language :
Whether rightly or wrongly, there exists a widespread opinion that due care is not exercised in Government expenditure. The feeling is daily growing stronger that the Government expenditure should be cut down and that the public estimates should be scrutinized and revised with a firmness never before exercised.
I submit that the hon. member for Colchester is right; expenditures must be cut down if we are to remain solvent, and in many cases they should be cut not with a blue pencil but with an axe. I submit, Sir, that up to this date there has been no sincere attempt on the part of the Government to carry out the views of my hon. friend the member for Colchester. You will find proof of this if you refer to the Estimates of the present year. Let me cite you one or two examples. The Government are proposing to vote for the Canadian Press, Limited, the sum of $50,000, and for the Canadian Associated Press $20,000, in all $70,000. I am opposed, Sir, to subsidizing the newspapers; I regard it as a vicious policy. The moment you begin to subsidize newspapers you strike a blow at their independence. There is the same objection to subsidizing the press as there is to subsidizing the church; both should be absolutely free. We are told that a similar amount will be contributed by the British Government. If that is so, Mr. Speaker, let me say distinctly that it is humiliating not only to the press of Canada but to the people as well to have the British taxpayers called upon to contribute money to the Canadian newspapers. Hon. gentlemen opposite say that Canada is a nation. Well, if so, let us act with becoming

dignity, and let the Canadian press deal with this matter as a business venture. What does my hon. friend the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) expect to get for this $70,000 of the people's money? I have no doubt that he expects to get $70,000 worth of propaganda. His plan is to teach the toddling public in Canada what they are to think about Imperial matters. Now, Sir, what is propaganda? I am not sure that I can give you a definition, but to speak frankly, my idea is that in a general way propaganda is tainted news, and the less we have of it the better. Sir, one grain of truth is worth a ton of propaganda. If, on the other hand, the object of the President of the Council is to strengthen the tie that binds us to the Old Country, then I say it is unnecessary. Those ties are already strong and they had better be left alone, we do not make them any stronger by talking about them. This constant chatter about loyalty to the Old Land and the old flag becomes tiresome and reminds me of Mark Twain's domestic hero, who boasted that he never jumped on his mother. Then we have such items in the Estimates as the following: Trent Valley Canal, $400,000; Toronto Harbour and Toronto Breakwater, $1,900,000; Canadian representation at Washington, $80,000; and scores of others. Now, these expenditures may be popular in the localities interested, and with an overflowing revenue there might be some justification for them; but no Canadian business would suffer if they were delayed for some time to come. Then again, we are asked to vote $150,000 for salaries and expenses of the Board of Commerce. I put it to you, .Sir: Is this a useful expenditure? Is this Board of Commerce worth $150,000 of the Canadian people's money? If it is not worth the money then let us dismiss the board and save that sum. Interest on war debt must be paid; our obligations to our soldiers and the dependents of the soldiers must be discharged ; but who will say that the Trent Valley Canal must now be built or that a playground must immediately be provided for the good people of Toronto? The taxpayers of the country are always willing to back up any productive enterprise, but they are not anxious to go to the poorhouse in .order to serve sectional interests. The people do not realize how their money is being spent. A gentleman talking to me the other day about this very point, said that if the Canadian taxpayer could come to Ottawa and see for himself how his money was being spent he would take an apoplectic fit. Now, Sir, I want to give a. few more
striking items. Here are one or two: Classification of the Civil Service, $108,173 57; New York News Agency, $30,000; one-half expense of Royal Commission relating to Indian Lands in British Columbia $317,797.68.

The Department
of Public Information was organized for political purposes and for no other purpose. The President of the Council gave it a high-sounding name, but that deceived nobody. The department proved to be very expensive, but when the facts were exposed at the last session of Parliament he himself became ashamed of it and promised that he would discontinue it. It lasted from the 9th day of November, 1917, until the 31st day of December, 1919. You will notice, Mr. Speaker, the significant date on which it started,-the 9th day of November, 1917. During that period this Department cost the country $200,986.54. Now, whatever value it may have had as a political agency

to assist the Union Government, he would be a bold man who would say that it was worth two hundred cents to the people of Canada. At the last session the President of the Council said that he would abolish it. Instead of abolishing it, as he said he would, he continued it under a new name. That fact is disclosed (by the following questions and answers:
Is Mr. M. E. Nichols, formerly Director of Public Information, still in the employ of the Government?
Mr. Rowell: Yes.
If so, what is his position, what are his duties, and what salary is he being paid?
Mr. Rowell: Director of Information, Department of External Affairs. Salary, $5,000 per annum.
Last year he was "Director of Public Information"; this year he is "Director of Information." The man is the same; the master is the same; the salary is the same; the duties are the same; everything is the same, except the name; he is now "Director of Information."
But that is not all. The President of the Council not only kept' the Department of Information alive under a new name; he started a new one in New York under Colonel John A. Cooper. A few weeks ago 1 asked for information about this new method of spending money and the minister in his reply referred me to an Order in Council dated July 17, 1919. I secured a copy of that Order in Council and it was disclosed, to my astonishment, that the money to pay the salary of this gentleman and his staff was improperly taken out of the money voted by Parliament' for war purposes. Let me read the Order in Council:

One thousand four hundred and eighty; I suppose that indicates the number of Orders in Council passed during 'the year up to that date.
Certified copy of a Report of the Committee of the Privy Council, approved by His Excellency the Governor General on the 17th July, 1919.
The Committee of the Privy Council, on the recommendation of the Right Honourable the Prime Minister, advise that pursuant to paragraph 4 of the Order in Council of the 24th February, 1919, P.C. 265-Lieutenant-Colonel John A. This is the point.
-of the office to be established for the purposes set forth in the said Order in Council of the 24th February, 1918, be paid out of the demobilization appropriation through the Department of External Affairs.
Rodolphe Boudreau,
Clerk of the Privy Council.
What is the date of that?

July 17, 1919. This money was voted for the defence and security of Canada and for the demobilization of our forces. Parliament was not told that any part of this vote would be used for the purpose of finding soft jobs for political favourites. This is a violation of a well-established principle, a principle that has prevailed in Great Britain since the days of Edward III, that money must 'be spent by the executive for the purpose for which that money was voted by Parliament and for no other. When I placed the question on the Order Paper I asked who this gentleman, Colonel John A. Cooper, was. I have since discovered that he is one of those vermiculating patriots who figured in the election of 1917. He was returning officer at Witley Camp, and when the ballot box over which he presided was opened it was discovered that it was stuffed with parcels of ballots that could not have possibly gone through the aperture. Over sixty per cent of the ballots in that box were illegally marked for constituencies in which the voters had no right to vote. You see, therefore, that it was necessary that something should be done to reward Colonel John A. Cooper. His job is to tell the American newspapers what smart men we have here in the Union Government. Here is a sample which appeared in a New York paper. I have no proof that this is from the pen of Colonel Cooper, but I suspect very strongly that it is. Anyway, this is how it reads:
That distinguished Canadian statesman, the Hon. N. W. Rowell, who is frequently mentioned as a probable successor to Sir Robert Borden, has arrived in the city en route to Washington, where he will represent Canada at the Labour Congress.

With reference to the proposed tariff changes, all I have to say is that they are very meagre. The concessions to the consumer are v.ery slight. There is not much in this Budget for the common man. His bread, his boots, his clothing, will not be any cheaper. The implements of production are still required to bear a very heavy burden. In camp-meeting parlance, which my hon. friend from Fraser Valley (Mr. Stacey) will understand, the concessions outlined in this Budget would he called "small mercies." I question very much if the farmer can be caught with that kind of chaff. Mr. Speaker, you have been brought up in town and are not as familiar with country life as I am, but no doubt you have been in the country sometimes on your holidays and you must have seen a farmer out in the pasture trying to catch a spirited horse with a handful of oats in his hat or in a tin basin. When he has caught the horse you must have seen him rub the horse's nose while he was getting the bit into his mouth and the throat strap securely buckled, and then pat him gently on the back preparatory to mounting him. I was just wondering if the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) could catch a low-tariff colt like my hon. friend from Strathcona (Mr. Douglas) or my hon. friend from Lethbridge (Mr. Buchanan) with such a shabby dishful of oats as this. Take instead the Liberal tariff platform. Here it is:
That the best interests of Canada demand that substantial reductions of the burdens of customs taxation be made with a view to the accomplishing of two purposes of the highest importance; First: diminishing the very high cost of living which presses so severely on the masses of the people; Second, reducing the cost of the instruments of production in the industries based on the natural resources of the Dominion, the vigorous development of which is essential to the progress and prosperity of our country.
That, to these ends, wheat, wheat flour and all products of wheat: the principal articles of food; farm implements and machinery; farm tractors, mining, flour and saw-mill machinery and repair parts thereof; rough and partly dressed lumber; gasoline, illuminating, lubricating and fuel oils; nets, net-twines and fishermen's equipments; cements and fertilizers, should be free from customs duties, as well as the raw material entering into the same.
That a revision downwards of the tariff should be made whereby substantial reductions
should be effected in the duties on wearing apparel and footwear, and on other articles of general consumption (other than luxuries), as well as on the raw material entering into the manufacture ofthe same.
That the British preference be increased to 50 per cent of the general tariff.
And the Liberal party hereby pledges itself to implement by legislation the provision of this resolution when returned to power.
That, Sir, is the platform on which I stand, and the platform which I shall submit to my electors if I am a candidate at th| next election. I regret that this platform does not meet the views of my hon. friend from Fraser Valley, although I understand he is a free trader in principle. The appeal he made last night on behalf of the British Columbia apple growers touched the hearts of hon. gentlemen opposite and he received a great deal of applause. I have been told that my hon. friend is a free trader in everything else excepting apples, but, as with our common ancestor while free trade is sound in principle, the temptation of the apple was too much for him. We fully recognize that the adoption of this tariff platform will result in a loss of revenue, but revenue must be secured and will be secured from some other source. This tariff platform is a great forward step and by taking this step at a time when revenue is so important the Liberal party have shown the courage of their convictions, and they have become to this extent the underwriters of progress and commercial freedom in this country.
But there is an even more important question than tariff reform, and that is the restoration of Parliamentary government in Canada. The election of 1917 was, to say the least, a very artificial affair. I do not believe the people of Canada had any idea at that time as to the kind of chicken they were hatching, and I believe they are now ready and anxious to rectify their mistake. Besides, Parliament, such as it is, is ignored, and the business of the country is carried on in secret conclave behind closed doors. The conclave itself has ceased to be a representative conclave. Our large French-speaking population is without representation in the Government, there being not a single cabinet minister, with the exception of the Prime Minister, from east of Montreal. It cannot be denied that this Government is hanging on to office without any mandate from the people. Unrest and distrust prevail to a greater degree than ever before. I submit that the remedy is a general election. Let the people decide. If the people are dis-



satisfied with this Government,
5 p.m. as I think they are, let them have an opportunity to turn the Government out bag and baggage and replace them with a Government in which they will have confidence. Confidence always counts for more than police forces and criminal penalties. Would not every sane man in Canada welcome a return to the conditions that existed during that golden period in our country's history from 1896 to 1911-a period when the land was first reserved for the settler, instead of being granted to great railroad companies; a period in which were carved out and started on their splendid career the western provinces; a period when the stranger within our gates was made welcome and treated like a free man in a free country; a period of overflowing surpluses, instead of bottomless deficits; a period when we built railways out of revenue and tax-exempt bonds were unknown; a period when letters were carried for two cents and the Post Office Department showed a handsome surplus; a period when profiteering was rare and the workingman could eat ibacon and eggs for breakfast and give his children butter instead of oleomargarine; a period when penal laws were few and the farmer's bee could stray into the sugar bowl without the farmer going to gaol for thirty days; a period when a man could blow his nose in 'his own way without asking the 'Secretary of State or the President of the Privy Council anything about it; a period when Parliament was consulted and Orders in Council were only resorted to in matters of routine; a period in which Canada first became known to the world as "daughter in her mother's house and mistress in her own." It was in short a period of fifteen years of good, clean, honest and progressive government. Is it any wonder, Mr. Speaker, that it is known as the golden period of Canada's history? Let us therefore ask the Canadian people whether they wish to perpetuate this present combination of decayed Conservatism and un-united Unionism, or whether they would prefer to place a new pilot in charge of the ship. Let the people decide, and we on this side of the House will cheerfully accept the verdict of the people, whatever that -verdict may be.

I said, Sir, there was a field open to the Government in the collection of taxation and I congratulate the Finance Minister that he has at last consented to adopt the American system. Two years ago when speaking during the Budget debate I urged the adoption of this system but apparently there was no desire to make collections promptly and to-day we find it is only applied, if I followed the minister correctly, to the income tax. The business profits tax will be collected, in the same old way.
I appreciate these profits may be very difficult to arrive at, but there should be clearly defined rulings governing depreciation, etc., printed and circulated, and whenever a ruling is made by the department publicity should be given to it through the press. The firm or corporation need not necessarily be named, but there should be uniformity, and then we would not have, as we have to-day, a feeling in the country that some firms are more generously treated than others. If this is done it will not be difficult for corporations to send in their cheques for 25 per cent of what they think they owe, and surely the account may be adjusted just as readily under these conditions as if no money accompanies the return.
Let me mention this year's experience in the First Michigan District-The Collector of Customs at Detroit is in charge ot income tax returns for this district, and the deputy collector informed me that by the 15th March this year they had filed with them 130,000 returns, covering incomes up to $5,000 per annum and 25,000 returns covering corporation taxes and amounts in excess of $5,000, and he further informed' me that of 130,000 returns of sums less than $5,000, 95 per cent of the tax payers paid the full yearly payment. Hon. gentlemen will appreciate what this means-the large amount of money that is immediately available to the Government of the country and the great saving effected in interest on money borrowed by the Government in order to carry on. In this country it did not matter that the man had the money to pay, he had to wait until he received his tax return. In the meantime his money was lying at the local bank perhaps without interest, and if interest were allowed, at most 3 per cent and the Government were paying the banks an increased rate for the money actually theirs but not available owing to the method of collection.

If the Minister of Finance is sincere and his department are actually trying to collect Business Profits and Income Taxes I would strongly urge a change in the proposed system to include business profits tax. As far as a reduction in the business profits tax is concerned I think it is a move in the right way. I believe the business profits tax contributes in no small degree to the high cost of living. It encourages extravagance upon the part of the manufacturer and adds unnessarily to the cost of output. Tax the income derived from manufacturing as high as you like. In the way I have suggested you will obtain revenue without interfering with the necessary growth and expansion of business.
In addition to imposing and collecting taxation it is equally the duty of the Government to carefully guard revenues and, wherever possible to eliminate unnecessary expense. What excuse is there for carrying on, say, the Board of Commerce? Here is a commission floating round the country at the public expense and, as far as the results go, practically Useless. It was absolutely absurd to appoint that board with a view of controlling prices. They could not hope to do that. Prices cannot be regulated artificially with any degree of success. The only way prices can be lowered is by production, and by the people recognizing that extravagance is a large factor in keeping them high. The Government should set the example. They should practice the greatest economy and cut out all unnecessary expense. No Board of Commerce can arbitrarily affect the situation, and I believe that board should be discharged at once. They are absolutely of no more use tfian a fifth wheel to a coach.
Take the Wheat Board, nobody knows what that has cost the country. It is true that hon. gentleman opposite say the Government are not paying the expense, but the people have to pay it in the long run and it makes no difference who issues the pay cheques. I do not know what is the attitude of our western friends with reference to this board, but I can say as far as the producers in our section are concerned they want none of it. We had rather a sad experience with the board in my constituency. Let me relate the circumstances: This year, after the United States Government lifted its embargo against Canadian wheat, I made an application on behalf of some of our farmers for permission to export about 3,000 bushels of wheat to the United States. After waiting approximately a month and getting two or three

answers that were rather contradictory, the reply finally came: No, we cannot permit you to export wheat. Now what were the conditions? There is no mill on the Canadian side within fifty miles of where these men live, and the Commercial Milling Company of Detroit were willing to buy. They had a paved road from their farms less than eight miles from Detroit-the price being paid by the Wheat Board was $1.90 and a participation certificate. The American mill offered to pay them from $2.35 to $2.59, which, with the exchange as it then stood, was as good as $2.90 per bushel, but the Wheat Board would not issue a permit. They took this attitude notwithstanding that our money was at a discount in the United States and we should have been glad of the opportunity of getting all the good American money we could. The Wheat Board insisted that the wheat would have to be shipped by rail and then exported in all probability to Greece or Rou-manit. to be paid for in the sweet by and by.
Is it any wonder the people of this country are dissatisfied and discontented? Today the price of Ontario wheat is, say, $1,95 with participation certificate. The Americans are paying $3 at Detroit with exchange, making the price $3.33.
Let me read you a letter on this subject which I received from one of our prominent farmers. It is as follows:
Tecumseh, May 11, 1920.
Dear Sir,-You will no doubt remember the efforts I have made to the Wheat Board to sell my wheat in Detroit and have so far been turned down.
It is not necessary for me here to give my opinion of the unjust treatment of the Wheat Board, especially this western part of Ontario, knowing that you are fully conversant with the conditions here and what we are up against. Not wishing to take up your valuable time, I will state the object of this note to you, and that is the following questions:
Can you tell if the Wheat Board releases their control of wheat in Ontario on the 1st of July next, and if not, can the balance unsold in farmers' hands of the 1919 wheat be sold with this year's crop and prices?
If I do not get an open market or a market price for my wheat I shall feed it to my stock.
If you can give me any information on the above questions I would be greatly obliged.
That is the way the Wheat Board stands in the estimation of the farmers in our district, and the Government would be well advised if they resolved to discontinue its operation. There is another board to which reference was made this afternoon by my good friend from Antigonish and Guys-borough (Mr. Sinclair), and that is the pub-licitj board that now exists in the city of New 'i ork. I understand from the Order in Council that it costs approximately $30,009 a year, and I could suggest to the Minister of Finanee a better way of spending that money, by which he would obtain far better results than keeping a bureau in the United States merely for the purpose of telling the people there what a great people we are. As I understand it, the duties of that board or commission consist in attending social gatherings and business meetings and telling people what the possibilities commercially and industrially of Canada are. Well, I can say, living close to the American border as I do, that generally speaking the American people, especially the business men, know pretty well what things are like in Canada, and particularly there is nothing . that affects our credit which they do not know. With that in view I am going to suggest to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance that he take that $30,000 and buy New7 York exchange with it and make good the promise of this country in so far as outstanding bonds are concerned. 1 am taking this matter up at the request of the bondholders of Detroit and also of bond salesmen of Windsor, who feel that something should be done. I would suggest to the minister that this is not a matter in connection with which one can adopt any ostrich-like policy. What the bankers of Detroit know to-day the bankers of New York know to-morrow, and what the bankers of New York know the investors of the United States know the day following. If we are going to hold up our credit in the United States and throughout the world, then the Government must handle this matter boldly, courageously and in a proper manner. Last fall we placed a loan of $300,000,000 and I have here a prospectus stating definitely and clearly that both principal and interest will be paid in gold. At the urgent solicitation of the Cen-

Windsor, May 14th, 1920.
W. C. Kennedy, M.P.,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Mr. Kennedy:
This Canadian Government of ours seems determined to keep me in hot water. You may recall that last Fall 1 wrote you relative to some unpleasantness that had arisen as a result of the sale of Canadian War Bonds to the President of one of the Savings Banks of Detroit.
When I approached this gentleman on the matter of purchasing these bonds he said, in effect: "Why, I don't want to buy bonds payable in depreciated currency." But, I countered glibly, "these bonds are payable in gold, both interest and principal. See, it says so right on the bonds, and my Government never violates or repudiates its pledges. downwards. If there are manufacturers in this country who are taking advantage of t'he tariff to extract the last five-oent piece from the consumer, then the Government should act and act quickly.
