Mr. Speaker, in rising to express my views on the Budget which is now before the House I wish at the outset to tender my sincere congratulations to the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) upon the honest and lucid statement he has given to the House of the country's financial condition at the present time and of the taxation which the people will have to bear this year. He has given us statements which have not been given in previous Budget speeches. In this matter he has shown that honesty of purpose which always characterized the more judicial statements which he made while chairman of the Railway Commission. While acting in that capacity he made a reputation for himself for honesty and clear judgment, and these same qualities were displayed in the speech he made when introducing the Budget. With the facts and figures he gave, some of which must be amazing to the people of Canada, he mingled patriotic expressions, and in noble language he expressed his gratitude to the returned soldiers, whom we must never forget now nor in the years to come. It was their courage and virtue which gave to Canada the fame she now enjoys among the nations of the world, and which contributed more than anything else to the great status apparently accorded this country by all the great nations. We owe our soldiers all possible gratitude. We shall never forget their energy, their valour, their heroism. We shall never for-

get Langemarck, where in the early days of the war the Canadian soldiers were left without reinforcements, but using the bodies of their comrades as a rampart withstood the attacks of the enemy until reinforcements came, and saved the day for Canada and the Empire. There are many other deeds of theirs which we might recall, but this is the battle we should never forget, because but for the Canadian soldiers on that occasion the war would have been lost, not only .to Canada and the Empire, but to Belgium and France, and to humanity. I was pleased, therefore, that te Minister of Finance did not forget to give expression to the sentiments of gratitude which we entertain towards our returned soldiers as well as towards the women of Canada who worked marvellously in every possible direction for their sons, brothers and husbands at the front with a spirit not only of loyalty and generosity but of Christianity, to help preserve the liberty and freedom we enjoy to-day.
There is one statement of the Minister of Finance to which I wish to call particular attention, and which I give him credit for having made, and that is his explanation of the discrepancy that exists between our net debt and our gross debt. That discrepancy amounts to $1,078,537,461.27, and the thinking people of Canada have been asking themselves for some time how it came to be so large, and whether it was really a fact or only imaginary. The Finance Minister has given the House to understand that a great portion of this discrepancy between our net and our gross debt is made up of investments which may not be realizable for many years to come, and some of them perhaps never, as he expressed it himself. He has shown that the net debt was $2,273,305,4.35, and the gross debt $3,014,483,774.12, the discrepancy being made up of loans and investments, a great many of which cannot be relied on as realizable.
I now turn to some of the details of the Budget, more particularly the taxes which the people of Canada will have to bear this year. No doubt the Minister of Finance has exercised his best efforts and best judgment to endeavour to relieve, if possible, the situation existing in the mind of the people of Canada. Of course, he has not been able to do all he would have wished to do. That would be impossible for any man in Canada in bringing down a Budget under the present conditions due to the terrible war. I had, however, expected more generous treatment from the Minister oi Finance for those who are less able to carry the burden of taxation. No doubt he has

done the best he could, but I am afraid that just before passing the threshold of the Council chamber when he was going in with his proposals he was told "Abandon hope," and consequently he has not been able to accomplish all he would like to do. He has given us, I think, the best perfected Tory Budget we have had in this country yet,- for this is a Tory Budget, more particularly as regards the taxes it imposes on the common people. We know that of the people of Canada, ninety-five per cent have to struggle for their living as against the five per cent who have in plenty the goods of this world.
There is one new tax which the minister has imposed to help to pay the debt of the country and the annual interest upon it, which struck me more particularly, and that is the sales tax. That tax hits, apparently, the manufacturer, the wholesaler and the dealer. One per cent has been added to the manufacturer's price. But the manufacturer and the wholesale dealer will add that tax of one per cent to the retailer's price, and the retailer will add that one per cent again to his price and he will take his profit on it. This will clean up everything and in the end it will be the consumer who will have to pay the tax of one per cent. Nobody else but the consumer will pay, whether the article be worth $1 or $10 or $100. The consumer has to pay the tax on everything that he buys. The soldier has had to pay the extra prices caused by profiteering in the textile and woollen business particularly since the war by being charged excessive prices for the suits of clothes- that he has had to buy since he came back from the field of battle. The minister has imposed a new tax on goods supposed to be needed by the common people, or by the people who are not endowed with the goods of this world, commencing with boots and shoes above $9. We know that $9 is a terrible price to pay for a pair of ordinary boots and shoes. It was a terribe price some years ago, but to-day we are confronted with the position that a pair of boots at $9 is only equivalent to a pair of boots that was selling at $3, $4 or $5 a few years ago. If the workingman wants to buy a pair of boots that will save his feet from the wet, the dust and the stones for a month or two, he will not do that by buying a pair of boots at $9. We know that a woman who wants to buy a pair of boots to wear while she is doing her work in the house, or while she is travelling on the streets or the roads in the country will have to pay more than $9. Therefore, the shoes which she will have to buy, being

above $9, will be subject to the tax; if she buys a pair at $4 or $5 they will only last a week or two because they are made of paper instead of leather. She is obliged to buy a pair of boots at $9 or over in order to economize as much as possible. Therefore, this is a new tax that will fall more particularly on the mass of the people. The same may be said in regard to the tax on clothing. No suit of clothes that, from the point of view of economy, is worth buying or wearing, is sold to-day under $45. This condition also applies to many other articles of clothing. This new tax which my hon. friend has imposed falls more particularly upon those who have the least means to pay it.
The tax on luxuries is certainly one which commends itself to my judgment. I have advocated it myself. The only doubtful thing about it is that we may make it so high that people will not purohase or import luxuries. I beg to congratulate my hon. friend upon his decision in this matter and to say that I approve of the tax on luxuries. The tax on imported liquors, wines and spirits may bring in a revenue for a year or so, but if Canada realizes our hope, as I trust it will, of becoming a temperance country, this tax will not bring in any great amount of revenue in the years to come.
Before proceeding to a general consideration of the Budget and of the fiscal question as it affects Canada to-day and will affect her in the future, I wish to say that I was amazed, this afternoon at the statements given by my hon. friend from An-tigonish and Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair). The facts and figures which he gave constituted an indictment against the Government, and it was certainly amazing that no one on the other side oif the House, not one of the ministers, not one of their supporters, rose to contradict, if a contradiction were possible at all, the indictment that will be carried by the wires throughout this country and outside of it. Certainly when these facts were so amazing I would have thought that some of the ministers would have got up and shown at least some resentment at their having been placed before the House. Although the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Siifton) was present, he listened to the indictment apparently with complacency notwithstanding that many of these statements were directed at his own department in connection with its management of the Printing Bureau. However, I am not familiar enough with the charges and figures brought forward by my hon. friend to discuss them at length and I only wish to express my disappointment at having heard no contradiction of the statements which he placed before the House.
Coming to the great question which occupies the minds of the people of Canada, the question as to the future, I wish, to ask the indulgence of the House for a few moments while I express a view that I have already expressed in this House and which I hold as firmly to-day as ever I did. I know it will not meet with the approval of my hon. friends on the other side of the House, and especially my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) if we are to judge him by the Budget which he has brought down. Meanwhile I wish to repeat on this occasion that, notwithstanding the adverse reports which strike our ears to-day, I am as much a free trader as ever I was. I am a free trader in principle, a free trader in theory and in practice. When I speak of free trade, permit me to say that I do not give expression to a mere opinion nor to a cherished idea; I speak the convictions which have grown firmer and firmer in my mind as a result of prolonged study of the question of protection and free trade as it has been developed from time to time in the different countries of the world.
I have arrived at my convictions as the result of a study of Adam Smith, Cobden, and Gladstone, and I am fortified in them by the views so strongly and courageously expressed by my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) whom I am pleased to see just now in his seat. That hon. gentleman has always been consistent, notwithstanding the conditions under which he at times has had to speak, in his advocacy of a free trade policy for Canada. In order to dispel any suspicions that might exist as to my adherence to that party let me say that it was my lot, whether for good or ill, to have lived for some seven or eight years in the city of New York in the eighties and the early nineties, at a time when Henry George, that great exponent of free trade, was exciting the admiration and the interest of the people of the United . States, and particularly those of the great city to which I have referred. It was my lot at that time to be able to follow his principle as personally expounded by him and to study them closely. I had the good fortune to hear Henry George address great audiences in the Cooper Institute. I have always borne in mind the expressions which I heard him utter at that time, and though his doctrines were slow in making their

way in the minds of the American people yet to-day they seem to he achieving the effect which was hoped for many years ago, and we now see a re-action in the public mind in the United States in favour of free trade. Sometimes doctrines may be enunciated ahead of their time, as one might say, and only with the passage of years do we see those ideas come to fruition. Henry GeoTge, as well as Cobden and Gladstone, in their respective periods, may have advocated principles that were then looked upon as too advanced; but free trade came to be accepted in England, and I hope that before long the same doctrine will conquer both in the United States and in Canada. It may be said that as yet free trade has not made much progress in Canada, not even in the ranks of the Liberal party. I admit that progress has been slow but a tree is of slow growth, even where the conditions are favourable, and the same may be said of free trade in this country. And then there is this also to be said. In the world of nature tornadoes and storms occur which often uproot trees from the soil. We had such a disturbance in the political life of this country in 1911, when an explosion of prejudice, for which the Conservative party were responsible, defeated the reciprocity agreement with the United States which the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier arranged after years of consideration and with the expectation of contributing greatly to the prosperity of the Canadian people. The defeat of the Reciprocity Act was a setback for the free trade idea. Reciprocity was worsted, with the result that ever since the people of Canada have been lamenting the fact. In the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta the sentiment in favour [DOT]of reciprocity was very pronounced, and this policy, which embodied the principle of free trade, would undoubtedly have been a great boon to them, as well as to the rest of Canada had it gone into effect. In the West a period of stagnation followed. In the city of Edmonton, when I was there in 1914, arrangements were put into effect to give employment to those who were in need. Works such as paving streets and constructing sidewalks in the outskirts of the city were undertaken in advance of the time when they would actually be required in order to give employment to workingmen who would otherwise have been objects of charity. Then take the matter of exchange between the United States and Canada. The adoption of the reciprocity pact would have given our farmers, more particularly those
f Mr. Turgeon.]
in the West, a market for their [DOT]wheat and other cereals, as well as for their live stock, and when any additions to that live stock were needed they could have been obtained from the other side without any difficulty. The trade that would have resulted between the two nations as a result of the reciprocity agreement would have been such as to have afforded an equilibrium in the matter of exchange, and we should not have suffered the loss in that regard which has taken place during the last year.
It has been said that the Liberal party have done very little to promote the adoption of free trade. I do not say that the Liberal Government, under the guidance o( Sir Wilfrid Laurier promised when they came to office in 1896 to establish free trade as it is in England immediately, but their aim was in that direction. Almost at the very first session of Parliament after their return to office their steps were turned in that direction, and as my hon. friend (:Mr. McKenzie) so lucidly explained yesterday, a great measure of relief was put into operation in 1897 which effected a saving to the people of $100,000,000 every year, and which to-day, bearing in mind the growth of population which has since taken place, would have represented something like $200,000,000 of relief from taxes yearly, a relief that would have been experienced more particularly by the labouring classes and the farming community. During all the intervening years, prosperity, contentment and happiness prevailed in Canada. The late Sir Wilfrid Laurier was all the time contemplating measures having for their object to relieve the people of further burdens. Finally he conceived that the best possible thing would be the inauguration of reciprocity with United States, and the then Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) my esteemed friend from Shelburne and Queen's spent an entire year in discussions with the American authorities and ultimately effected an agreement which commanded the admiration of everybody who has had the opportunity of studying it and who was conversant with the natural conditions as between Canada and the United States.
Let me now for a moment or two consider some statements which have been published in the press of Canada, more particularly the Government press. The effort is being made to make all possible capital out of exaggerated reports of a so-called cleavage in policy between two sections of the Liberal party. Under scare heads some of the newspapers hold up to the public eye the so-called spectacle of a party divided into moderate protectionists and moderate free

traders. These journals allege that the speeches made in. Parliament and out oi it indicate that there has been a departure from the tariff plank as laid down in the Liberal platform, and that the ideal of free trade is being forsaken. The truth may seem funny to lips that have been tasting gall and wormwood, but these journals greatly deceive themselves. We still keep the ideal in our mind, but, as I have already explained, conditions are not always favourable for carrying an ideal into effect. So it is with the Liberal party. Actual circumstances make concessions imperative, and events are gradually leading up to a demonstration of the fact that in the last analysis 'free trade must solve the problems that confront us. It is my intention to support the amendment of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr.. Fielding), and I shall do so with pleasure. I see in it a sincere expression of a desire to alleviate the burdens which bear so heavily upon the shoulders of the poor consumers of this country. The amendment of the hon. gentleman proposes a step in the right direction and I shall therefore willingly support it. I need not read to this House the resolutions which were passed toy the Liberal party at its convention in August last, tout I think 1 can safely say that the amendment moved by the hon. member is in harmony with the proposals contained in those resolutions. I have no doubt whatever that the public will view the amendment as a wise one, and I know that when the Liberal party comes into power, whether it be in three months' or three years' time, one of their first considerations will toe the affording of some real relief for the poor people of this country.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that our friends in the Farmers' party cannot find any considerable difference between their platform and ours, for if I read their programme aright, it is contained in the policy of the Liberal party. But, whatever differences there may toe beltween us, we are at any rate, in accord in this, that we have a common desire to free the masses Of the people of Canada from the burden which has been imposed upon them [DOT] for so long by the protectionist policy that has been in vogue in this country; and I think it is also, our common desire that that relief shall soon be given to the people.
With regard to our home industries, I may say just a word or two. Some years ago when the National Policy was being launched by Sir John A. Macdonald, that statesman said that we should look after
native industry in its infancy. Well, the native industries of Canada are now forty-five years old. I think that the Conservative leader, Sir John A. Macdonald, intended that they should be propped up only so long as they were incapable of taking care of themselves, and I think that if he could return to earth now and see what progress Canada has made since he departed this life, if he could see some of our so-called infant industries, he would tell his friends on the other side that if these industries still need to be propped up, then they had better remove such cripples from the highway and let the chariots of prosperity and liberty pass on their way. The Conservatives or the Protectionists, Mr. Speaker, have changed the description which they have all along applied to their protege; it is now "home" industry, not "native" industry; they think that home industry appeals more to the imagination of the people. I think, Mr. Speaker, that it is a poor country that restricts its efforts in any direction, industrially, commercially or agriculturally, and looks only to the home market. I say that the manufacturers and all others engaged in business should not be satisfied with the home market alone; they must look to foreign markets which are now open to them but which they may lose to the more vigilant American producer or the more alert German .trader who is now preparing to take full advantage of all the markets which the world can offer. These highly efficient business men are invading the field while Canada is marking time and, if I may say so, execrating the term "free trade." I think, Sir, that the conditions which are prevailing at the present time are conducive to free trade. I may be in error, but I think that the people of this country, and indeed of all countries, have never been in a better position to adopt a free trade policy in the exchange of products than they are to-day. What are we called upon to do at the present moment? We hear on every hand that the increased production of foodstuffs is imperative for the safety of the world. As most of you probably know, Dr. J. W. Robertson has travelled extensively in Europe since the conclusion of the war. He .appeals to the people of Canada to produce .and to export in order to afford some relief to the present distressing conditions under which the people of many European countries are living. When I think of the lack of food, the lack of proper clothing, the lack of many of the essentials of life which the

people of these European countries are suffering, I feel that I should ask our farmers, in the West and elsewhere, to produce, to stay on the farm, to keep their sons and their daughters on the farm. I would have them free from taxes, municipal, provincial, federal, in order that we may be able to do our part in bringing about the salvation of suffering European countries. The condition there is almost as siad as it was when the world was in the midst of war, because millions of children are dying from the effects of starvation, an indirect result of the war. Therefore I say to every farmer and to every man of industry: take away all tariff from these implements of industry; take away all tariff or encumbrance upon what the farmer needs in his work of production. I do not ask that in the interests of the farmer alone; I want him to be able to produce, and the cheaper you make his production the more he will produce and the more of our products will go across the ocean.
It was with sadness that I listened the other night to my genial friend from St. John City (Mr. Elkin) in his reference to what the farmers had done and what cause they had for complaint. The farmer who gave his son whom he could spare from the farm and who kept another son at home in order that he might be able to assist in production of the necessities of life to maintain our soldier companions in the field did more than my hon. friend, with all the thousands of dollars which he may have given and which I am sure he did give- his sacrifice was not as great as that of the farmer who gave his son and himself remained on the farm to engage in the great work of production.
My hon. friend talked also of protection. He was a free trader, he said; now he is a .protectionist. Of course, I do not know his motives, but his conversion has been very rapid. Three years ago he was elected to this House as a Liberal joining the Liberal-Unionists as a sacrifice for the time being, as a matter of conscience. With his attitude on that occasion I do not quarrel. But he says he is a protectionist because Canada is not in a position to adopt free trade. He tells the farmers of his province to be satisfied with the conditions that he and the industrial people of his city or of other cities impose upon them. He would give them no say in the making of the future of Canada; he would have them come very modestly into the streets and market squares of St. John with their products and be satisfied with what the industrial people
give them. They should listen only to my hon. friend and hie fellow protectionists; hand over their products; and wait for the future. But, Sir, the farmers have been as generous as any other class of people, according to their means. To-day, I say, is the time more than ever when the industries of Canada can go in the direction of free trade, because their products are sought, as are the products of Canadian farms, in every part of the world. Every financier who looks into the matter dispassionately encourages the industries of Canada to produce and to take advantage of the market that offers for, their products, just as it offers for the products of the farm. Last April the directors of the Bank of Montreal announced an issue of $2,000,000 new capital stock to be offered to their shareholders of record as at the close of business on May 20, 1920, at 150 per share in the ratio of one in ten in order that the manufacturers of Canada might be able to take advantage of the trade that offers to them in the West Indies, British Guiana and West Africa. This bank with other important banks has announced the policy of forming close connection with permanent institutions firmly established rather than that of opening branches in foreign countries with all the resulting expense and difficulty. The banks are prepared to offer to the manufacturer further credit in order that they may take advantage of these markets which are offering to them.
A few days ago a lady who was the guest of the Ottawa Kiwanis Club at the Chateau Laurier, Miss Jill Crossley-Batt, told her hearers that Australia is in need of the products of Canada and is desirous of establishing trade communications in order to receive those products. She said also that Australia has products to offer to us which we greatly need, such as wool, leather, and raw materials in connection therewith, through the lack of which the people of Canada have had to pay excessive prices for clothing and shoes. It is urged by some that because we are a small country; because our population is only eight millions, we are not in a position to attend
9 p.m. to the demands of the foreign market. But if there is a country that is suited to the adoption of free trade at the present time it is Canada. We have immense resources. We can produce more pulp and paper than any other country in the world. We have vast water-powers awaiting only the hand of the engineer in order to produce every day millions of dollars' worth of articles which the Old World needs. We have many other kinds

have to be paid by the consumer; it has to be paid, as I have already said, by ninety-five per cent of the population of the country who are least able to support it. I repeat, every time you tax production you raise the selling price and increase the cost of living. It is not so with a tax on land. We therefore change a burden into a benefit to the people. By taxing land values the owner finds his land unused and he will sell it cheaper than under the present system. Under the present system those who use land in a productive manner are taxed more heavily and their improvements are taxed. The more they improve their property and extend their field of production the more they are taxed. But we are asking to tax land on the value given it by the community. The community would judge that a farm, or a piece of land on the outskirts of a city, was worth so much today. The tax would be imposed on that value, and whatever improvements were made would be free. It would encourage the owner to improve his property or, if he does not improve his property, to sell. That system would bring immigration, it would bring settlers to those immense tracts of vacant land which we have in the West and to many abandoned farms in the East, and to areas in the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, which have been left' uncultivated. Under this system these farms would immediately become productive. It would bring in capital and create a demand for labour both of which are now debarred because of the excessive prices asked by speculators. Our farmers in the country and our homesteaders in the West have everything to gain by this tax on land values.
During the war the very thing which should have been taxed was not taxed and everything which was taxed should not have been taxed. To-day we have a heavier debt to pay and more annual interest. The income tax has also been delayed. 1 cannot hold my hon. friend the Minister of Finance responsible for that because he was not in the House or a member of the Government. But I remember an eloquent appeal made in favour of the income tax at a special session of the House, which only lasted about five days after the declaration of war, when the hon. member for Bed Deer rose and called upon the Government of Canada immediately to impose an income tax upon the people in order to form an asset against the expenditure on account of the war. We, on this side of the House, all joined him, but for two or three long sessions the then Minister of Finance (Sir
fMr. Turgeen.]
Thomas White) smiled away our efforts for the taxation of incomes. At last, late in the session of 1917, after having said at the beginning of the session the collection of the tax would not pay the expenses of collecting it, the income tax was adopted.
I demonstrated at the time that even amongst his colleagues in the Cabinet there were a sufficient number of millionaires to be able to guarantee the expense of the collection of the tax throughout Canada, and therefore he need not be uneasy as to the cost of making that collection. At last, in 1917, the Government acceded to our request. But it took us a long time to obtain the concession.
The Government may also set up the claim that they have adopted other measures calculated to promote the welfare of the country. They may say that in 1917 they gave free wheat also. But an election was anticipated shortly and such was the feeling that had been aroused among the people who were bemoaning and lamenting the defeat of the reciprocity pact, that some western ministers who had been paying a visit to the West got alarmed, and returned to Ottawa and said, "We must have free wheat." But free wheat, as well as the concession in regard to income tax of which I have spoken, are measures which wefe really due to the exertions of the Liberal party.
I wish again to urge the adoption of a policy of taxing land values. The inauguration of this system may take some time- perhaps that is to be expected in the case of every new system of taxation-but it is only a few days since we were informed by Mr. Breadner, the Commissioner of Taxation that even after three years the methods of collecting the income tax were not perfect, and that two or more years might yet elapse before the system was adjusted to a nicety, so that collections might be promptly made and at a great lessening of expense. The same perhaps would be true if a system of taxing land values were adopted. But, notwithstanding any difficulties which might have to be overcome at its inception, we would within a very few years derive a revenue from it of $100,000,000, and even $200,000,000, which would wipe out a considerable portion of the war debt, and compel future generations to admit that we had lifted 'from their shoulders some of the burdens imposed. May I not appeal to my generous friend, the new Minister of Finance, and ask him in the most amiable manner that I can, to take into consideration this question of taxing land

values, and see if he cannot give effect to it before this vote is taken, or at a later stage when we go into committee. It is doubtless unnecessary to inform the Minister of Finance-who follows these matters perhaps more closely than I do-as to what happened in England with respect to this policy. In the British Parliament, owing to a snap verdict the movement for the taxation of land values received a temporary set back, but this fact did not discourage Mr. Asquith. That right hon. gentleman expressed no despair over what had happened. It was, he said, not an occasion to write the epitaph "Requiescat," but rather "Resurgam"-"I shall rise again." And when that takes place a better day will dawn for the mass of workers in Great Britain. The temporary defeat of this policy is no doubt attributable to the peers of England who are great land owners and have taken the opportunity to rid themselves of this taxation and have the burden placed on the industries of Great Britain.
Last year a tariff inquiry was promised by the Minister of Finance, but no inquiry has yet taken place. To-day we again have the promise of such an inquiry. I have all belief in the sincerity of the present Minister of Finance and I hope his anticipation will be realized. But he will need to be on his guard against the manufacturers and the other protectionists who will come to him with a demand not for additional duties perhaps, but for "moderate protection" the idea of which was so eloquently set forth toy my genial and good-hearted friend the Minister of Marine (Mr. Ballan-tyne). The same idea of a "moderate" tariff was expounded in the West sometime ago by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen). "A moderate tariff," what a vague expression it is ! You might erect a Chinese wall around the confines of Canada and yet the protectionist would tell you it was "moderate" protection. The promise of "moderate protection" is not satisfactory, we want something more definite. People will tell you, "What we want is a scientific tariff," and this term is freely used in the public journals of Canada. We are not given any figures to show what a "scientific" tariff means; it is capable of almost any interpretation. I hope therefore that when the Minister of Finance comes to sit down at the table and deal with the so-called "scientific tariff" he will display the same courage that animated him in presenting his Budget which could not have been in conformity with his hopes or expectations. As a matter of fact science 169
is opposed to a tariff. Science in its operation works for the good of humanity and contributes to the welfare and comfort of the community. In this instance the community consists of ninety-five per cent of the community who toil for a living. They are the persons in whose behalf science should be invoked and the protectionist should be told plainly, "We will took after the mass of the people first." The tariff, Mr. Speaker, is only a creation of the convenience of the privileged classes, and I must protest against any further' impositions on the people.
(Now, I feel that I have taken up too much time and have encroached on your patience, Mr. Speaker, and the patience of the House. But I could not let this occasion pass without expressing my view of conditions as they are to-day. We are living under abnormal conditions; abnormal conditions prevail throughout the world; and it is for that very reason that we must courageously face the situation and adopt the best possible means at our disposal for restoring the happiness and prosperity of this country and helping, as far as lies within our power, to restore the happiness and prosperity of those countries in Europe which are appealing to Canada and to the United States for sustenance. Now, exclusive attention to home markets cannot possibly meet those conditions. We must have an expansion of trade if we are not only to develop our own resources but help those countries that are suffering as a result oi the war.
I have spoken at great length, Mr. Speaker, but what I have said has come from the heart. I have given utterance to what I hold to be truths and not mere pet ideas. I trust therefore that what I have said will have some weight with the Minister of Finance, and that that hon. gentleman will not regard my remarks as mere idle talk to keep this House occupied for the time being. I have expressed my convictions and I feel that I am right. I believe, Sir, that the truths I have stated will appeal not only to my own constituency but to all the people who do not believe in privilege.

I am not going to speak at any great length. Perhaps I have not as much to say as my hon. friend who has just sat down (Mr. Turgeon), and at all events I will try to express my views in very much shorter time. I should like to add my congratulations to those that have been already expressed to the Minister of Finance for the



very able Budget he has presented and the clear manner in which he has presented it. I do this, Sir, with a great deal of pleasure, because I can look back thirty years to a time when the present Finance Minister and myself were associated in another form of public service. I think it was his first position in the public service as a young man just entering his profession. He made good in that position, Sir, and it has been my pleasure to see him advance from one post to another, each more important than the last, until to-day he occupies one of the highest places in the Dominion of Canada. My thirty years of friendship and acquaintance with the minister therefore makes that fact a very gratifying one to me. The minister displayed in his speech the characteristics he has always exhibited since I have known him-caution in preparing his case and courage in presenting it. Evidently he learned a good while ago that old maxim: Be sure you are right, then go ahead; and the result i.s that in this Budget he has shown, as I think, a more courageous course than any Minister of Finance that we have had in the Dominion of Canada. Of course, he and the Government face to-day the most difficult conditions that any Government or any Finance Minister ever had to face in the history of Canada. There have been times in the past when a large amount of money had to be raised; but never has there been a time when such a tremendous volume of revenue was demanded, never was there a time when circumstances called for such large expenditures; never were we compelled to impose such drastic taxation, taxation so new and to which the people are so unaccustomed.
Taxation that, in my judgment, it required a great deal of courage for the Government to impose. The minister has told us the truth and the whole truth about our national assets, and I think he is to be commended on that score. He has resisted the temptation to make our balance sheet appear better than it is, and that is not always done by public men when they are trying to put the best face possible upon the case they are presenting to the country. I believe 'that the frankness displayed by the minister in that respect will be received with admiration by the people of Canada. I think that the people like their public men to be frank and straightforward. They can see through any camouflage that is put on just as easily as those who are behind the scenes; and any short experience in public life leads me to believe that if a man has a case which he

can defend the people are ready to listen to him. They are reasonable in meeting their obligations and will respond to courageous leadership. But to my mind, the confidence which the Minister of Finance displays in the Canadian people all through his speech is the best and truest note he 'has sounded, and I venture to predict iiha't the nation will respond and be prepared for any necessary sacrifice. He has added burdens of taxation as undreamt of in the past as they are imperative for the present and for the immediate future, and he has called for united effort to meet the obligations of to-day and reduce the liabilities of to-morrow. This should, and I believe it will, inspire our citizens to give him 'the support he needs to begin the process of restoring the finances of this country to their pre-war solidity.
As I see it, Mr. Speaker, the Budget shows high regard for the masses. It may bear somewhat heavily upon wealth, upon those large incomes, but in my judgment that is the right kind of Budget to bring down in any country, particularly in these times qf stress. What I was particularly interested in was his declaration that the Government will adhere to the principles of the National Policy. I am confident that that will appeal to the judgment of the great mass of the people of Canada. I desire especially to emphasize his pledge that the tariff shall not be used to exploit the consumer. I will not take the time, Mr. Speaker, to read all that he said on this subject; I shall simply quote a few words from page 2569 of unrevised Hansard. The Finance Minister said:
Apart from the question of revenue, the tariff should have regard to the maintenance, stability and prosperity of Canadian enterprise in the development of all our natural resources in lands, forests, mines, fisheries, as well as our agricultural and manufacturing industries.
That, as I understand, is the principle of the National Policy. He goes on to say:
Consideration must also he given to the importance of creating and maintaining conditions that will afford to Canadian industrial workers opportunities for steady and remunerative employment. It is undoubtedly in the true interests of Canada as a whole that Canadian workers should not be forced to seek in foreign countries employment and opportunity denied them at home by reason of the export of the natural resources, primary products, and raw materials with which the Dominion is amply endowed.
Mr. Speaker, I am satisfied that seventy-five per cent of the people of Canada are in favour of the protection of our industries. An intensive propaganda has been carried on for years to convince them that the

manufacturers systematically exploit them to accumulate huge fortunes. In a few instances huge fortunes may have been piled up as the result of-taking advantage of the tariff. But I venture to say that that ha's happened only in isolated cases; that the men who work in factories as well as those who manage these enterprises have equally been beneficiaries of the protection that has been given to our industries.
Mr. Speaker I am a protectionist by conviction. I am not like some men in public life; I did not inherit my politics. My father was an intimate personal friend of and sympathizer with the grandfather of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), the late William Lyon Mackenzie.
Hear, hear.

He was a Baldwin reformer, and he instructed me in the doctrines of Liberalism of that day and until I grew up to be a young man. He was not satisfied to call himself a reformer; he was a Clear Grit, a follower of Brown and Mackenzie. You will readily understand, Mr. Speaker, that growing up beside a man holding such political views, I was somewhat thoroughly instructed.
And the son went astray.

Well, I am just coming to that. I grew to manhood cherishing a very high regard for Brown, Mackenzie, Blake and Mowat. But about the time I was called upon to cast my first ballot in a Federal election the late Sir John A. .Macdonald introduced the National Policy and affirmed the principle of the protection of our industries. I had grown up, Sir with conditions surrounding me that upset all .my preconceived theories about the tariff. As a boy and a young man I saw my schoolmates, as they grew to manhood and learned their trade or profession, forced to go across to the United States to get employment. I saw the largest furniture factory in Canada at that time, located in Toronto, forced to close its doors and throw two thousand men out of employment. I saw trade sales of American-made furniture put on every week in Toronto the effect of which was to drive out the furniture factories we had in that city and close down one of our great industries. There were more Canadians in Chicago then than there were in Toronto or in Montreal. The very .best blood of Canada, our young enterprising men, unable to find opportunities in out own country, were obliged to go * across the border in order to earn their livelihood. I sav. Mr. Speaker, 169J
that any young man of observant mind growing up in those days could not help being impressed with such a spectacle as that which I am trying to describe. So, when I was called upon to cast my first vote in a federal election I decided that nothing could be worse than what we had and that I was willing to give the new policy a trial. I voted for the National Policy, and I have voted for the party that supported the National Policy and protection ever since because my (subsequent observation and experience confirmed me in the belief that protection of our industries is absolutely necessary for the further development of Canada. I suppose I am like one of those whom the member for West Kent (Mr. McCoig) spoke of this afternoon. He complained that the member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) had a short time ago advocated free trade and reciprocity. Well, I never was quite guilty of that, but I was wondering while the member for West Kent was referring to the member for Parkdale why he did not couple the name of that hon. gentleman with that of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), who has changed his views in regard to the tariff quite as much and in quite as striking a way as has the member for Parkdale.
Now, the tariff is necessary for our urban communities;-I think many free traders will acknowledge that-and it is equally necessary for Tural communities, for the farmers and their sons and daughters. If this country is ever to be great it can only be by the establishment of diversified industries. If a farmer in Ontario has six sons, only one will stay on the farm; the others - will want to go elsewhere, to be doctors, lawyers, mechanics or business men. If we have not large urban communities such as are developed and maintained by large industries, there are no opportunities for men who want to leave the farm and en-'ce in other professions; and that is one of the primary reasons why the farmers of Ontario are protectionists. They have always voted for a protectionist policy, and my judgment is that they are as soundly convinced as they ever have been that that is the best policy for Canada. It has brought hundreds of millions of dollars of American capital into this country; it has kept hundreds of thousands of Canadians at home. We need our young men, Mr. Speaker, to develop our national life. We want our young men and our young women to build up their homes in this country and to give their work and their service to the building up of the nation.

There are some things which have not been done in Canada in which, I think, we might have made greater advances. In passing, I should like to say that we are not proceeding fast enough with thS development of our fuel resources. The time is coming, and indeed is not far distant, when the question will be, not how much we have to pay for coal, but whether we can get coal at all, and the primary duty of the Government is to develop not only our coal resources but our peat resources and any other fuel resources we have, and to establish such means of transportation as will make it possible for us to bring coal from the extremes of the country into the central provinces. I might talk at length upon that subject, but I want to keep my promise to you, Sir, that I would not be long, and I have something else to say.
I appreciate very much, as I think the people of Canada will, the desire of the Government to economize in every possible way. I have not yet seen many signs of economy. One action has been taken which effects a considerable saving, and my suggestion is that it should be carried out to a much larger degree than it has been already. I listened with great interest to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), when he spoke of the Civil Service of this country. He said that it was necessary that the expenditure on that service should be lessened. He told us that there were forty or fifty thousand men and women in the service; that it was a great organization through which the Government carried out its enterprises and its administration, and that millions 'of dollars could be wasted and spent uselessly through an inefficient Civil Service throughout the country, which millions could equally well be saved through efficient organization and thorough co-operation amongst the members of the Civil Service. I am not sure that that declaration by the Minister of Trade and Commerce received the attention that it deserves, and I am going to propose to him, to the Prime Minister, and to the Government, a way by which they can effect a saving of $20,000,000 a year.
My first suggestion would be that the Government declare a holiday of one year in the making of new appointments to the public service of this Dominion. If there are positions to fill, let the Government promote some of the superfluous members of the service in the various departments and place them where it is supposed that new officials are required. In that way, I be-

lieve <with 'the exception of the few experts that might f>e required) the Dominion service could run for a year without one additional appointment. This is what has been done in one department. At long last, as some hon. member said, we got a Secretary of State who had the courage to go into the Printing Bureau, the condition of which branch of the service had been a disgrace for years. There was not a printer in Canada who did not know how grossly that department was overloaded; that hundreds of thousands of dollars were being wasted every year. And yet it seemed to be impossible to find a man who would assume the position of minister of that department and clean it up as it ought to be cleaned up. This House knows that it has been decided to cut off three or four hundred men, and three hundred men have already been cut off from the Printing Bureau. At the present rate of wages in the allied printing trades, I would estimate that that would mean a saving of between $500,000 and $600,000 a year. With three hundred men cut off and $500,000 saved a year, as much work is being got out of that department to-day as was got out of it when there were thre hundred more men on the staff. And the same thing can be done in practically every other department of the Government of Canada. But courage is required for measures of that kind, and I am going to credit every minister of the Government with having courage to do ftiis, and say to him: You can save $20,000,000 if you will collectively go through every department of Government in Canada as the former Secretary of State went through the Printing Bureau, and I believe that by transferring unnecessary officials in one department to necessary positions in another department, we can get along for a year without making aiiy new appointments, except such technical and expert officials as may be required. That is the way to get efficiency. Make it possible for industrious men and women to work for promotion. Why is it that in the Printing Bureau a staff of men and women, three hundred less than it was a month or so ago, is turning out as much work as before? It is because those who remain know that they must work in order to hold their jobs. Let that idea go all through the service of Canada, and two men would do the work that three men are doing now. But some person must take the matter in hand and do it with a spirit of courage that is not always manifested in the administration of departments. It is not necessary that I should state to the House that the service of Canada is over-

loaded. There is not a member of Parliament, nor a person working in the Civil Service, nor a minister of the Crown, who does not know that. I say: Take the overload and distribute it around; instead.of making new appointments, promote those who are now in the service, and if they are not fully qualified, give them an opportunity to qualify so that they can go up from one position to another. Form a board of deputy ministers for the promotion of efficiency in the Civil Service, and let them collaborate in regard to every position that falls vacant or every appointment that is to be made, instead of, as at present, if an official is superannuated or dies, putting a new man in his place although there may be in the department a dozen or fifty persons more than are necessary to carry on the work. A good deal more would have been accomplished if instead of the cumbersome system that has been adopted, some kind of instruction had been provided for those who are now in the service, so that a man or a woman could qualify for the position higher up, thus, having always ready those who could take their promotion for any positions that became vacant. Tf yon could inspire the deputy ministers and the assistant deputy ministers with the idea that they were going to make the public service of Canada the most efficient public service in the world, there would be competition from the bottom to the top and from the top down to the bottom amongst those who are now in the service in order that they might render better service, earn a better reward and get a better position. What inducement is there now for a man or u woman who is in the service to show extraordinary ability ot industry''- There is no inducement whatever; too many of them simply put in their time, and many of them who do that could be turned into good officials if some incentive were put before them to inspire them to give better service.
There is another feature of this case that deserves attention. Why not readjust the hours of the officials of this Government? Why not require them to work eight instead of six and a half hours a day? Why not add 20 per cent to the working time and reduce the staff 20 per cent? Manifestly, if you increase the time that is put in by the employees in the public service in Ottawa by 20 per cent, you can do with 20 per cent fewer employees. There should be no objection to any person who works for this Government putting in eight hours a day. Why should not a clerk or a messenger work ei ht hours as well as a bricklayer, printer, moulder or any other man?
That is one v;ay in which practically 20 per cent more of service could be given to this country by these employees, and a saving of 20 per cent on about $75,000,000 or $80,000,000 would be an enormous sum left in the treasury of this country. It would mean both better officials for the service and a great many more million dollars to the country.
But this is a task that calls for the best brains you have in the administration. It calls for the best brains you have in the service, for men who have been long in the service, who understand its needs, and who would enter into the idea sympathetically and apply themselves to give their very best to working ou't this plan for the benefit of the people of Canada. I do not think it is a task for a group of glib-tongued young theorists who come into a country they have never lived in, of whose system of Government they are entirely ignorant, and who bring in some theories that may be applicable elsewhere and, in effect, put those theories over and above the experience of deputy ministers and chief officials who have been in the service of thia country for thirty or forty years. If you had such a plan as that in operation, you would not have a spectacle such as that which was presented in the Senate a few days ago, when a debate took [DOT] place on the appointment or dismissal of a translator who had been appointed by the present Commission and who was found after two and a half months to be absolutely unable to translate two or three pages of the debates in the Senate. He received higher marks in the written examination than anybody else, but when put down 'to do the job he could not translate two or three pages olf Hansard properly in two and a half months. That is the kind of thing you are getting now, and it is not making for efficiency in the service. I think the present plan takes the heart out of responsible deputy ministers. My idea would be to inspire them to give their very best to this country, to go through their departments, and to go through them collectively and discuss with each other: Where is a man to fill this position and that position? It would also put heart in the officials in minor positions, who, I am sure, with the hope of promotion, would be willing not only to work eight hours a day, but to work harder and more efficiently while they are working. The Government is calling on the people of Canada to practice economy, "Produce and Save" is the watchword. Well, I submit that here is a plan that will effect econo-

my, and I submit it with all due deference. I am not submitting it with any complaint against the Government; I know the extraordinary labours the ministers have had to perform during the years of the war, and in fact up to the present time; they have been worked to death. I am not complaining, but I am afraid they have not thought of this plan, and I have thought of it; so I am just putting it before them for their consideration, and am wondering whether they will themselves do through the Government and through this House what they are calling on the people of Canada to do, namely, to practise the closest economy in our expenditures.
There is reason to congratulate the Government upon its Budget. It shows great courage to impose these new taxes. I think those taxes are going to bring in more than enough money to meet all the expenditures of this country during this fiscal year, and I think there will be a substantial sum besides to apply in reducing the debt. It is not an easy thing to impose new taxes, but I want the Government to go a little further now that they have imposed them. Let them get to work and, after the most careful thought, devise a plan somewhat on the lines I have suggested for reducing the service by 20 per cent and saving $20,000,000 additional to apply to the reduction of the public debt.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to refer to one remark which was made by the hon. member who has just taken' his seat (Mr. Hoek-en), in respect to emigration from this country previous to the adoption by the Government of Canada of the National Policy. I was a boy some years, I expect, after the hon. gentleman was, and -for many years after the old National Policy had been given what I would consider a fair trial in this country, and I would point out to him that there was great emigration from this country even in those days. Many of our young people were leaving the farms of Canada and going to the United States. Right at the present time people are leaving the farms in the province of Ontario in hundreds. You have fewer farmers on the land in Ontario to-day by many thousands than you had ten years ago. Now, if protection as we had it under the old National Policy was such a good thing for the farmers of this province, it seems to me that instead of having fewer farmers we would have more farmers on the land.
iMay I ask a question?
Does the hon. gentleman pretend to speak for the province of Saskatchewan?
Sure.

Very different was the [DOT]action of the minister's predecessor who, though convinced of the justice of our claim, made promises which he did not live up to. If I have erred in taking upon myself something that I should not have done, I must say that I am only following in the footsteps of the hon. gentleman (Mr. H. A. Mackie) who undertakes to speak not only for the province of AlbeTta but for the whole Dominion of Canada when he gets a chance.
Now I wish to pay some attention to the speech of the hon. member for St. John city (Mr. Elkin). That hon. member came to this House as a Liberal and an avowed free trader. When, in the discussions around the corridors, the question came up as to who among the Liberals would stick to the Government forces, the hon. member for St. John city was one who was always counted out because, as I have said, he came to this House as an avowed free
26G6

trader. What then was the surprise of hon. members on this side-in fact 1 think of hon. members on both sides-when the hon. member rose in his place a few evenings [DOT]'go and delivered one of the strongest protectionist speeches I have heard here.
Honest conviction.

There is always a reason for such a quick conversion, and looking for the reason in the case of the hon. member for St. John one is reminded, Sir, that in private life he is a manufacturer and that his manufacturing business is one that is listed to be included in the great merger that is now in the process of consummation in this country. We have often heard, Sir, that the monied men of Canada-and, I think, of every other country-carry their politics in their pocket. Would it be that there was a money consideration in connection with this quick change of heart as exemplified by the hon. member for St. John? We have proof that men in the financial life of this country do change their politics in a hurry when they think there is a chance of their pocket being touched. I point you to the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) who with a number of other wealthy men of the city of Toronto-many of them reputed to be millionaires-repudiated their old party and its policy in 1911 because they, in their short-sightedness, feared to pit their ability against that of the Yankees in a fair, open, and above-board business transaction. No matter what the cause we have in the hon. member for St. John a living example of one who, in the twinkling of an eye, has been transformed from an avowed free trader into an ardent protectionist. One might understand how a moderate protectionist could extend, or stretch his moderate views so that he would get into the class that might be termed protectionist for protection's sake, or stand for the principle of protection, but how a man can go to bed at night an avowed free trader and wake up in the morning a real high protectionist is beyond my limited powers of comprehension.
You did it for fifteen years.

As I said the hon. member for St. John was an avowed free trader because he used these words in his address to the House the other evening:
I believed in tree trade once myself.
Those were the hon. gentleman's words. It would be interesting for the House to

know just when the hon. member experienced his change of heart. He says he was once a free trader but does not enlighten the House as to when he was converted. Is it not a fact that the hon. member, as I have already said, has been engaged in manufacturing for a considerable time and that when so engaged he was a free trader? But now that his business is being absorbed in the gigantic merger to which I have alluded his fear of American competition is such that he has changed from a free trader to a protectionist. When the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) a few days ago moved the adjournment of the House so that we might consider this merger many felt that something should be done by way of investigating the reasons for that combination and its effect, if consummated, upon the commercial life of this country. I think there is something in connection with this matter that would stand a thorough investigation. You will notice that the hon. member said the western free trader does not exist to-day, but he drew attention in those words to the demands of the western grain growers:
The western grain growers who want to make immediate and sweeping reductions in the tariff are fond of picturing Canadian manufacturers as a small group of selfish men, who support the tariff policy solely in their own interests. These grain growers ask: why should this privileged class be permitted to levy toll on all other classes in this country?
Yes, Mr. Speaker, the grain growers do picture the supporters of high protection as ,a selfish class. It has been proved times without number that the Canadian manufacturer can and does compete in the foreign market, where he has no protection against the products from other countries. Why then are the Canadian people penalized when our manufacturers can compete outside of Canada without protection? Is it not a reasonable question to ask, and logical to claim that they can compete in Canada? The grain growers not only claim that the manufacturers are selfish in asking for protection that they do not need, but they also claim that the manufacturers are standing in the way of the advancement and development of the agricultural resources of this country. Again I would remind the House of the resolution adopted by the Conservatives at the Toronto meeting in which they said that no handicap of any kind should be allowed to impede the progress of our farmers. Is there an honourable member in this House who will argue that you are not retarding the progress and development of

agriculture in this country by imposing a tariff on the importation of agricultural machinery and thereby enabling the Canadian manufacturers to exact the amount of that duty from the farmers? Is this not a restriction on production? Any one who has given the matter of Canadian finances any serious thought must realize that the one big thing needed in Canada to-day is increased production so that the heavy taxes .incurred through our war effort will not bear jtoo heavily on the producer. If this Government would adopt the resolution as passed by the Conservatives at Toronto their first consideration should be to remove all duties on agricultural implements and machinery necessary to production. The honourable member for St. John then gives to the House his unsupported word that the protective tariff not only benefits the manufacturer but almost every-other class in the country and then goes on to enumerate a long list. In this connection let me say that I am quite willing to leave this matter in the hands of the residents of the urban centres for them to decide upon at the next general election. Regarding taxes and the farmers the hon. member has this to say:
It should be the aim of Parliament to remedy every legitimate grievance, giving attention first to those that are most pressing. If the case of the farmers is to be given priority, then let the farmers show some cause more convincing than the loudness of the howl they are putting up. What taxes do they pay to swell the federal revenues other than those levied by means of the tariff? When other people are paying taxes under the tariff, and income and profit taxes besides, how do the farmers Justify their demand that they be relieved of taxes altogether? If their grievance is a real one, how do they account for the fact that there is such a brisk demand for western farm land, with advancing prices? If there were a movement away from the land there would be some colour to their argument.
Mr. Speaker, this is the first intimation that I have ever had that the farmers of this country were trying to evade paying their taxes. The farmer pays the general taxation of this country the same as every other person, and he pays the income when his income comes within the taxable amount. It is true that he has not been taxed for excessive profits because he never gets into that class. Regarding the other matter o>f a brisk demand for western farm lands, and a movement towards the land, I admit that there is a great cry of " Back to the land," but I fail to see any evidence of the urban dwellers of this country making any move towards the land. Any farm lands that are being taken up in Western Canada to-day are being taken principally by Americans
from across the line, or by farmers in that country enlarging their holdings. In this connection I would like to say that in the province of Saskatchewan, from which 1 come, there are fewer actual farmers on the land to-day than there have been homesteads entered for.
As a fitting climax to the other mis-statements of the hon. member for St. John he winds up in this fashion: in respect to the representation in this Parliament:
If the farmer persists in an attempt to get from under altogether, and leave the whole load to be carried by the townsman, it is not unlikely that the latter will arise in his might and sweep aside the pernicious principle whereby he has been deprived of his just representation and voting power.
The hon. gentlemen proceeds to give some comparative tables in respect to this matter, which tables I shall not quote. If the farmer dominates in this Parliament, Mr. Speaker, it is not by force of numbers. It is a well-known fact that according to the last census taken in this country 54.5 of our population were found to be rural, and the farmers in this Parliament represent much less than twenty per cent of the total membership. I think, therefore, that this statement of the hon. member for St. John is on a par with many other statements he has made. The hon. gentleman makes the threat that if the farmers continue to raise what he is pleased to term " a howl," the urban dwellers may rise in their might and demand that they be give:, representation in this Parliament in strict accordance with population. I do not think that any farmer in this Parliament has ever suggested that the farmers should be represented in this House other than by population. If some of the rural ridings do not contain as many electors as some of the urban constituencies, I believe that the reason is that in re-distributing the country some consideration was given to area.. But if my hon. friend and those new-found friends of his see fit to make a re-distribution of the country and adhere strictly to population they will hear no complaints from the farmers.
Again, we as western farmers are charged with wishing to market our grain in Minneapolis and Chicago, and to buy our machinery from the United States. The only reason for this is that the western farmer wants to market his grain in Minneapolis and Chicago at times when it will bring him more money. There is no matter of sentiment in connection with the question at all. And the same applies to the purchasing of machinery. If any man needs a

piece of machinery and he can buy it for less money in the United States he naturally buys it there, and I think that a large portion of the machinery used in the factories of this country by people who support a protective tariff will be found to have been purchased in the United States. Yet no one would think of claiming that the owners of the factories are less Canadian because they use American machinery. There are those people in this country, Mr. Speaker, who consider that in buying American made machinery they are really doing a service to Canada, for the amount of the tariff levied on the machinery they get goes directly into the public treasury and not into the pockets of the manufacturers.
I come now to the last of the statements made by the hon. member for St. John, and this is in respect to our railways. He says:
These railways were trailt with the money of the people of Canada in order that there might he opened up for settlement a territory whose population are now enjoying marked prosperity. Without the railways there would have been no West. Without the taxes cheerfully paid year after year by Canadians in the East there would have been no railways. Is the partnership arrangement that has proven so mutually profitable now to be terminated simply because of the unwillingness of the West to pay its share of the operating expenses?
Did you ever hear a more ridiculous statement made in this House, that the farmers, residents of this country, taxpayers in this country, with everything they own subject to the advancement and development of this country, were out to cripple the great transportation system that we as a people now own and are operating? No argument can be adduced to combat a statement of this kind for it is .foundationless and absurd. In respect to this railway problem, let me say, the people of Western Canada are prepared to pay their full share of the deficit on these roads, but they are not willing that the whole deficit should be borne by those who use the roads, and they will not submit to an increase of freight rates for this purpose. I hold, Mr. Speaker, that this Parliament as representative of all parts of this Dominion and all the people of this Dominion, is responsible for the sad muddle in connection with our railways and we Western Canadians hold that it is not just or fair that those who happen to use these lines should be penalized for the mistakes of this Parliament as representative of all the people. I am forced to think, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member could not have heard the hon.

Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) when he gave these words to the House last session. They will be found at page 69, Vol. 1:
As a western representative, and particularly as a representative of the province of Saskatchewan, I feel I should say one word more. I refer to the conditions existing in Western Canada, where all the elements of disunion exists- A pretty big and serious problem. I am referring now to the tariff cleavage between East and West. You know, we might as well look that squarely in the face and recognize the situation as it exists; there is no use dodging it, that situation is there. What are the people of Canada going to do? Can it be settled in some way or another? Is there a possibility of a settlement? There is no doubt as to the feeling out West. There is no division among the people. All parties are practically united. What is to be done? You will have an opportunity later in the session to consider the question. In the meantime, I simply wish to point out to this House, and to the people of this country, that that is one of the other questions on the horizon that in many ways looks dangerous ; at any rate it divides the people of this country and puts them in two hostile camps, fighting against each other all the time. If Canada is to be what we hope it shall be, then an honest and earnest attempt must be made to solve that problem which stares us squarely in the face.
These were serious words coming from one who should know conditions in Western Canada, and yet we have an hon. member going out of his way, I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, at the request of some western politician, to make statements in this House that can serve no good purpose but will have, if taken seriously, a disrupting effect. I have taken considerable time in dealing with the remarks of the hon. member for St. John, and I now wish to say to him and to the House that the people of Western Canada are just as loyal to Canada, her institutions and the grand Empire of which we form a part, as the hon. member from St-. John, or any of those new friends whom he has so lately adopted.
Last year, Mr. Speaker, most of us who are now on these cross benches were called upon to make a decision in respect to the proposals of the Government in its Budget. The proposals did not suit some of us, and the promise of the ex-Minister of Finance for a revision of the tariff was not taken seriously. We had little hope, even with a commission appointed, that the tariff would be revised downward to such an extent that our views would be met. We voted against the Government on that occasion, and I think that in view of the result as we have it before the House to-day, our judgment was sound. My own reasoning was that there was no chance of the ex-Minister of Fin-

ance (Sir Thomas White) agreeing to a reduction that would suit me, and even if he did, I had little hope of its getting by a party caucus when the great majority of those present would be opposed. That was my opinion and in consequence, I have since been a cross-bencher in this House.
I would like to state my position in respect to the policy that we cross-benchers have adopted. It has been the aim of many hon. members of this House to make it appear that this movement is simply a class movement. Many of them have taken occasion to look over the policy as laid down by the Canadian Council of Agriculture and have tried to make the people believe that this policy is purely of a class nature. I may say that in 1916, shortly after this policy had been adopted by the Canadian Council of Agriculture, every candidate in the federal field in Saskatchewan was circularized by the secretary of the Grain Growers' Association there and asked whether if elected, he would be prepared to support the policy as laid down by the Canadian Council of Agriculture. My reply was in the affirmative, and prior to the consummation of Union Government in the fall of 1917 I issued a manifesto to the electors of Last Mountain in which I stated that I was a supporter of that policy in respect of tariff matters. I stated my position in this House in the Budget debate of last session. In view of these facts and the stand I had taken ever since I first became interested in public affairs, I could do nothing less than vote against the Government proposals as contained in last year's Budget. There are those who took a different view. It is for them to say whether the Government has fulfilled its pledges and whether the proposals of the Government as contained in this year's Budget are in the interests of Western Canada.
I am not going to make any appeals to the Government, Mr. Speaker; I believe it would avail me very little to do so. But I wish to point out to them that to have a solid, a lasting prosperity in this country, it must be founded upon the accomplishments and life of the agriculturist. Make prosperous the condition and happy the home life of the farmers in this country and all else will be well. There need be no worry about paying our national debt. Canada has the resources; her people have the conquering spirit. Change the fiscal policy so that no handicap shall be placed upon the real producers of wealth in this .country. But to do that, Mr. Speaker, to
bring about that change, we must, in my opinion, have a change of government.
There are many other matters to which reference might be made, but the hour is late and I do not wish to tire hon. gentlemen. I may say here that in respect to the matter of an early election I voted for the resolution of the hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) at the beginning of this session, and I did so believing that I was carrying out the wishes of my constituents. I believe that the great majority of the electors of this country have lost confidence in the Government. It matters not whether it is a good government or a bad government, the people who are rseponsible for the election of members to this House are dissatisfied, and I believe that they have every reason to be dissatisfied. This Government was elected for a specific purpose and for a definite period. The purpose was to win the war; the period was for the length of time that it would take to accomplish that purpose. That has all been accomplished, and the people -are demanding that there should be an appeal to them. There are other reasons. This Government came into being as a Union Government. The promise was made to the people and to the Liberals who joined with the Conservatives under a Conservative leader that there should be a fifty-fifty split as respects the personnel of the Cabinet. That pledge or promise has never been fulfilled; and to-day we have a Government dominated by high protectionists. For this reason, I believe it is up to this Government to conclude the business of this session and then to appeal to the country for a new mandate.
On motion of Mr. M. Clark (Red Deer) the debate was adjourned.
